cards.explain: Recognize critical chain when a scenario mentions buffers and resource-constrained paths; safety is removed from individual estimates and pooled into project and feeding buffers.

cards.back: Time reserved to protect the project completion date against variability.
cards.explain: Placed at the end of the critical chain, the project buffer absorbs delays, and its burn rate tells the PM whether intervention is needed.

cards.back: Time protecting the critical chain from delays on noncritical paths.
cards.explain: Feeding buffers sit where noncritical chains join the critical chain, so a late feeder path consumes buffer instead of pushing the critical chain out.

cards.back: Modeling many possible outcomes using probability distributions to estimate overall schedule or cost uncertainty.
cards.explain: Monte Carlo runs thousands of iterations to produce a probability distribution, letting the PM say things like there is an 80 percent chance of finishing by June.

cards.back: Defines how project costs will be estimated, budgeted, monitored, and controlled.
cards.explain: Part of the project management plan, it sets units of measure, precision levels, control thresholds, and EVM rules before any cost estimating begins.

cards.back: An approximation of the monetary resources required to complete an activity or project.
cards.explain: Estimates should include a range and are refined over time, for example a rough order of magnitude estimate of minus 25 to plus 75 percent.

cards.back: An approved time-phased budget used to measure cost performance, excluding management reserves.
cards.explain: The cost baseline includes contingency reserves for identified risks but excludes management reserve, and its cumulative S-curve is the PV used in EVM.

cards.back: Total authorized funding, generally including the cost baseline and management reserve.
cards.explain: Remember that cost baseline plus management reserve equals project budget, so using the portion outside the baseline needs management approval.

cards.back: The total budgeted value of the work in the project performance measurement baseline.
cards.explain: BAC equals total planned value at project end and is the starting point for forecasts such as EAC and variance at completion.

cards.back: Budget or time set aside for identified risks and their potential effects.
cards.explain: Contingency reserve covers known-unknowns, sits inside the cost baseline, and is typically controlled by the project manager when an identified risk occurs.

cards.back: Budget held for unforeseen work within project scope, outside the cost baseline.
cards.explain: Management reserve covers unknown-unknowns, sits outside the cost baseline, and using it requires management approval plus a baseline update through change control.

cards.back: A cost directly attributable to project work, such as assigned labor or materials.
cards.explain: Direct costs are charged straight to the project, such as wages for contractors working only on it, whereas indirect costs are shared overhead allocated across projects.

cards.back: A cost supporting multiple activities or projects, such as administrative overhead.
cards.explain: Indirect costs like office rent or corporate IT support are spread across many projects, so they are allocated to your project rather than traced to it.

cards.back: A cost that does not vary with the amount of project output within a relevant range.
cards.explain: Fixed costs stay the same whether you produce more or less, such as a monthly equipment rental or a one-time license fee.

cards.back: A cost that changes based on production, usage, or activity volume.
cards.explain: Variable costs scale with volume, such as materials or hourly labor, so a scope increase raises them while fixed costs stay flat.

cards.back: Spending on assets that provide value over multiple accounting periods.
cards.explain: CapEx buys long-lived assets like servers or buildings that are depreciated over time, unlike OpEx, which is expensed in the period it occurs.

cards.back: Spending required for ordinary ongoing business operations.
cards.explain: OpEx covers recurring running costs such as subscriptions, utilities, and support staff, which is why moving to cloud services shifts spending from CapEx to OpEx.

cards.back: Considering all costs throughout a product's life, including acquisition, operations, maintenance, and disposal.
cards.explain: Life cycle costing can favor a pricier option with lower maintenance and operating costs, supporting decisions beyond the cheapest upfront purchase price.

cards.back: A performance measurement method integrating scope, schedule, and cost.
cards.explain: EVM combines PV, EV, and AC to show whether the project is ahead or behind schedule and over or under budget, and to forecast final cost.

cards.back: The authorized budget for work scheduled to be completed by a point in time.
cards.explain: Planned value answers how much work should be done by now in budget terms, and total PV at project end equals BAC.

cards.back: The budgeted value of work actually completed.
cards.explain: Earned value is the key input to every EVM formula: calculate it as percent complete times BAC, then compare it to PV and AC.

cards.back: The actual expenditure incurred for performed work.
cards.explain: Actual cost is what you really spent, so compare it to EV, not PV, when judging cost performance.

cards.back: The difference between earned value and actual cost.
cards.explain: CV equals EV minus AC; a negative result means over budget, a positive result means under budget, and the formula always starts with EV.

cards.back: The difference between earned value and planned value, measured in budget units.
cards.explain: SV equals EV minus PV; negative means behind schedule, and it returns to zero at project end because EV eventually equals PV.

cards.back: A measure of cost efficiency, calculated by dividing EV by AC.
cards.explain: CPI below 1 means you get less than a dollar of work per dollar spent, so over budget, while above 1 means under budget.

cards.back: A measure of schedule performance, calculated by dividing EV by PV.
cards.explain: SPI below 1 means behind schedule and above 1 means ahead, but SPI measures earned work and does not show whether critical-path activities are on time.

cards.back: The forecast total cost of the project at completion.
cards.explain: Pick the EAC formula by scenario: BAC divided by CPI when current performance will continue, or AC plus a new ETC when original estimates were flawed.

cards.back: The estimated additional cost required to finish remaining work.
cards.explain: ETC is what is left to spend from now, while EAC is the total including money already spent, so EAC equals AC plus ETC.

cards.back: The difference between the original budget at completion and the forecast cost.
cards.explain: VAC equals BAC minus EAC; a negative VAC means the project is forecast to finish over budget, like CV but for the whole project.

cards.back: The cost efficiency needed on remaining work to meet a specified financial target.
cards.explain: TCPI above 1 means remaining work must be done more efficiently than planned; compare it to current CPI to judge whether the target is realistic.

cards.back: Aligning planned project expenditures with available funding limits.
cards.explain: Funding limit reconciliation may force rescheduling when funds arrive in tranches, shifting activities so spending in a period does not exceed approved funds.

cards.back: A projection of money expected to enter and leave the project over time.
cards.explain: Use the cash flow forecast to spot periods where spending exceeds incoming funds, which may trigger funding limit reconciliation or schedule changes.

cards.back: Combining activity or work package cost estimates into higher-level budgets.
cards.explain: Cost aggregation rolls estimates upward from work packages to control accounts to the whole project, building the cost baseline when determining the budget.

cards.back: Monitoring, allocating, and controlling funds held for uncertainty.
cards.explain: Track reserve drawdown against remaining risk, releasing contingency as identified risks pass and escalating when remaining reserves look insufficient.

cards.back: The degree to which characteristics of a deliverable fulfill requirements.
cards.explain: Quality differs from grade: a basic, low-grade product with few features can still be high quality if it meets its requirements without defects.

cards.back: Defines quality objectives, standards, processes, responsibilities, and controls.
cards.explain: As a subsidiary plan, it answers scenario questions about which standards apply, who performs quality activities, and which metrics define acceptable results.

cards.back: Activities focused on providing confidence that appropriate processes will produce quality outcomes.
cards.explain: QA is proactive and process-focused, like auditing whether testing procedures are followed, while QC inspects the actual deliverables for defects.

cards.back: Activities evaluating deliverables to determine whether they meet quality requirements.
cards.explain: QC is reactive and product-focused, like testing a build for defects, and the verified deliverables it produces then go to Validate Scope for acceptance.

cards.back: Translating the quality management plan into executable quality activities and improving project processes.
cards.explain: It is the PMBOK process that performs quality assurance, using audits and process analysis to improve how work is done rather than inspecting outputs.

cards.back: Monitoring and recording the results of quality activities to assess performance and deliverable conformity.
cards.explain: Control Quality produces verified deliverables, which then move to Validate Scope where the customer or sponsor formally accepts them.

cards.back: The total cost of achieving quality plus the costs caused by poor quality.
cards.explain: Investing more in prevention and appraisal usually reduces the much larger cost of failures, which is PMI's argument for building quality in early.

cards.back: Spending to prevent defects or evaluate whether requirements have been met.
cards.explain: Remember it as money spent to get it right, prevention plus appraisal, such as training, documentation, testing, and inspections.

cards.back: Costs resulting from failures, defects, rework, or unmet requirements.
cards.explain: Remember it as money lost because things went wrong, internal plus external failure, such as rework, scrap, warranty claims, and lost customers.

cards.back: Spending to avoid errors before they occur, such as training or process design.
cards.explain: Prevention is the cheapest place to spend on quality, because training, better design, and process standards stop defects before they exist.

cards.back: Spending to evaluate or inspect quality, such as testing and audits.
cards.explain: Appraisal finds defects but does not prevent them, so testing and inspection count here while training and process design count as prevention.

cards.back: The cost of defects identified before delivery to the customer.
cards.explain: Rework, scrap, and retesting caught by the team before release land here, whereas complaints, recalls, and warranty work after release are external failures.

cards.back: The cost of defects discovered after delivery to the customer.
cards.explain: Usually the most expensive category, because it adds lost reputation, liability, and customer goodwill on top of the repair cost itself.

cards.back: An independent or structured evaluation of compliance with quality practices, processes, or requirements.
cards.explain: Audits review processes rather than individual products, so they belong to Manage Quality and help find nonconforming practices and spread good ones.

cards.back: Examination of a deliverable to determine whether it meets specified criteria.
cards.explain: Inspection examines the product itself and sits in Control Quality, whereas a quality audit reviews whether processes are being followed.

cards.back: A bar chart organizing problems by frequency or impact, often used to identify the vital few causes.
cards.explain: Based on the 80/20 rule, bars are sorted from highest to lowest so the team fixes the few causes responsible for most defects.

cards.back: A cause-and-effect diagram used to explore possible causes of a problem.
cards.explain: Use it in brainstorming scenarios to explore possible causes; it suggests causes but does not show how often each occurs, which is a Pareto chart's job.

cards.back: A graph showing process performance over time relative to statistical control limits.
cards.explain: A process is out of control when a point falls outside the control limits or seven consecutive points fall on one side of the mean.

cards.back: Statistical boundaries used to identify unusual variation in a process.
cards.explain: Control limits come from process data, typically three standard deviations from the mean, while specification limits come from customer requirements.

cards.back: Boundaries defining acceptable product or service characteristics based on requirements.
cards.explain: They are set by the customer or contract, not by process data, so a stable process can still produce output outside specification limits.

cards.back: A graph showing observations over time to identify trends or patterns.
cards.explain: A run chart is like a control chart without control limits, useful for spotting trends but not for judging statistical control.

cards.back: A chart showing the frequency distribution of numerical data.
cards.explain: Histograms show the shape and spread of data, while a Pareto chart is a sorted histogram of categories used to prioritize causes.

cards.back: A graph used to explore relationships between two variables.
cards.explain: Use it to test whether two variables move together, like defects and overtime hours, remembering that a visible correlation does not prove causation.

cards.back: A structured form used to collect and tally observations.
cards.explain: Also called a tally sheet, it gathers raw defect counts where the work happens, and that data often feeds a Pareto chart or histogram.

cards.back: A diagram showing the steps, sequence, and decisions within a process.
cards.explain: Flowcharts help reveal where defects or delays can enter a process, and the SIPOC diagram is a common high-level form of one.

cards.back: A data-driven approach focused on reducing process variation and defects.
cards.explain: Six Sigma aims for near-perfect output of only a few defects per million opportunities and uses DMAIC as its standard improvement method.

cards.back: Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control; a structured process improvement approach.
cards.explain: The final Control step sustains the gains, which distinguishes DMAIC from a one-time fix; it is Six Sigma's counterpart to the PDCA cycle.

cards.back: An iterative cycle for testing and implementing improvements.
cards.explain: Associated with Shewhart and Deming, it underpins continuous improvement: try a small change, check the results, then standardize it or adjust.

cards.back: Comparing processes or results with reference standards or other organizations to identify improvements.
cards.explain: For example, comparing your defect rate with an industry leader's sets realistic targets and reveals practices worth adopting.

cards.back: The ongoing effort to improve efficiency, performance, quality, or outcomes.
cards.explain: In agile it shows up as retrospectives, and in Lean as kaizen, both making small frequent improvements rather than waiting for big overhauls.

cards.back: An uncertain event or condition that could positively or negatively affect project objectives.
cards.explain: On the exam a risk is always future and uncertain; once it happens it becomes an issue, and remember risks include upside opportunities, not just threats.

cards.back: A risk with a potential negative impact.
cards.explain: Threat responses are escalate, avoid, transfer, mitigate, or accept, so when a scenario describes something bad that might happen, choose from these rather than opportunity strategies.

cards.back: A risk with a potential positive impact.
cards.explain: Opportunity responses mirror threat ones: escalate, exploit, share, enhance, or accept, for example seizing a chance to finish early by reusing a vendor's existing component.

cards.back: A current problem or condition requiring action, rather than a future uncertainty.
cards.explain: Exam clue words like 'has occurred' or 'is now happening' signal an issue, which goes in the issue log and needs resolution, not a risk response plan.

cards.back: Defines how risks will be identified, analyzed, responded to, and monitored.
cards.explain: Created early in planning, it sets methodology, roles, funding, timing, risk categories, and probability-impact definitions, but it does not list the individual risks themselves.

cards.back: A record of identified risks, assessments, owners, responses, and related information.
cards.explain: The register lists individual risks one by one while the risk management plan describes the process, so check or update the register first when a scenario mentions a specific risk.

cards.back: A summary of overall project risk exposure and important individual risks.
cards.explain: Unlike the register's risk-by-risk detail, the risk report summarizes sources of overall project risk and key individual risks for stakeholders and sponsors.

cards.back: The person accountable for monitoring a risk and coordinating its response.
cards.explain: The owner need not perform the response personally; they watch the triggers and ensure the agreed response is carried out, and each risk gets a single named owner.

cards.back: The degree of uncertainty an organization or stakeholder is willing to accept in pursuit of objectives.
cards.explain: Appetite is the broad attitude toward taking risk, while tolerance and thresholds turn it into measurable limits, such as accepting no more than a 5% cost overrun.

cards.back: The acceptable level or range of variation from objectives.
cards.explain: Tolerance is the acceptable band, like plus or minus 10% on budget, whereas appetite is the general willingness to take risk and the threshold is the trigger point.

cards.back: A specific level of risk exposure that triggers action or escalation.
cards.explain: Thresholds make appetite measurable, for example any risk with more than $50,000 impact must be escalated to the sponsor, so crossing one tells the PM to act.

cards.back: The likelihood that a risk will occur.
cards.explain: Probability is rated on scales defined in the risk management plan and combined with impact on the probability-impact matrix to prioritize risks during qualitative analysis.

cards.back: The effect a risk would have on project objectives if it occurred.
cards.explain: Impact is assessed against each objective separately, such as cost, schedule, scope, and quality, and pairing it with probability determines a risk's priority.

cards.back: A grid used to prioritize risks according to likelihood and consequences.
cards.explain: A qualitative analysis tool where risks landing in the high-probability, high-impact red zone get priority responses, while low-low risks go on a watch list.

cards.back: Evaluating and prioritizing risks using relative ratings and contextual characteristics.
cards.explain: Qualitative analysis is fast, subjective, and done for nearly every risk to prioritize them, whereas quantitative analysis is numeric and reserved for top risks or overall risk.

cards.back: Numerically analyzing uncertainty and its effects on project objectives.
cards.explain: Look for numeric techniques such as Monte Carlo simulation, EMV, decision trees, or tornado diagrams, and remember it is usually reserved for large or complex projects.

cards.back: The probability-weighted monetary value of a potential outcome.
cards.explain: A 30% chance of a $10,000 loss gives an EMV of negative $3,000; summing risk EMVs helps size contingency reserves and drives decision tree choices.

cards.back: A diagram-based method for evaluating alternative decisions and uncertain outcomes.
cards.explain: Calculate EMV along each branch, include the cost of each decision, and choose the path with the best expected value, such as build versus buy under uncertain demand.

cards.back: Assessing how changes in individual variables affect an outcome.
cards.explain: Sensitivity analysis identifies which individual risks or variables most drive variability in the outcome, and its results are typically displayed as a tornado diagram.

cards.back: A chart ranking uncertain variables according to their influence on results.
cards.explain: The widest bar at the top marks the variable with the greatest influence on the outcome, so that is where risk responses and attention should focus first.

cards.back: The potential effect of uncertainty, often expressed through probability and impact.
cards.explain: Exposure aggregates risks, so the PM compares total exposure against thresholds to decide whether the project's risk level is acceptable or needs further responses.

cards.back: A warning sign or event indicating that a particular risk may occur or has occurred.
cards.explain: Triggers are recorded in the risk register so the owner knows exactly when to activate the contingency plan, for example a vendor missing two delivery dates in a row.

cards.back: Risk remaining after responses have been implemented.
cards.explain: Residual risk is expected and planned for, often covered by contingency reserve, unlike a secondary risk, which is a new risk created by the response itself.

cards.back: A new risk arising as a direct result of implementing a risk response.
cards.explain: Hiring a subcontractor to mitigate a skills gap creates a new risk that the subcontractor delivers late, while residual risk is what remains of the original threat.

cards.back: Transferring responsibility for a risk decision to an appropriate higher authority.
cards.explain: Escalate when a threat or opportunity is outside project scope or beyond the PM's authority; once escalated, it is owned at program, portfolio, or organization level.

cards.back: A predefined action to implement if a particular risk event or condition occurs.
cards.explain: Planned in advance and activated by a trigger, it differs from a fallback plan, which is the backup used if the contingency plan itself fails.

cards.back: An alternative response used when the original risk response proves ineffective.
cards.explain: Think plan B for the response: the contingency plan runs first, and the fallback plan is invoked only when that primary response does not work.

cards.back: An unplanned response developed to address an issue or risk that has materialized.
cards.explain: Workarounds are unplanned and reactive, used when unidentified or passively accepted risks occur, unlike contingency plans, which were defined before the event happened.

cards.back: Eliminating a threat or protecting the project from its potential consequences.
cards.explain: Avoidance changes the plan to remove the threat entirely, such as dropping a risky feature or extending the schedule, while mitigation only reduces probability or impact.

cards.back: Reducing the probability or impact of a threat.
cards.explain: Mitigation lowers the odds or the damage but the threat remains, such as adding extra testing, whereas avoidance removes the threat or its cause entirely.

cards.back: Shifting financial or response responsibility for a threat to a third party, often through insurance or contracts.
cards.explain: Transfer moves ownership and impact to a third party without eliminating the threat, usually for a premium, with insurance, bonds, warranties, and fixed-price contracts as classic examples.

cards.back: Acknowledging a risk without taking proactive action beyond agreed monitoring or contingency arrangements.
cards.explain: Active acceptance sets aside contingency reserve while passive acceptance just reviews the risk periodically, and it suits low-priority risks or those with no cost-effective response.

cards.back: Taking action to ensure a positive risk opportunity occurs.
cards.explain: Exploit is the opportunity counterpart of avoid, removing uncertainty so the upside definitely happens, such as assigning the most skilled staff to finish early.

cards.back: Increasing the probability or benefit of an opportunity.
cards.explain: Enhance is the opportunity counterpart of mitigate, raising odds or benefit without guaranteeing it, unlike exploit, which aims to make the opportunity certain.

cards.back: Allocating ownership of an opportunity to a party better positioned to realize it.
cards.explain: Sharing mirrors transfer for opportunities, such as forming a joint venture or partnership with a firm that can capture a benefit the project cannot achieve alone.

cards.back: Tracking identified risks, identifying new risks, and evaluating response effectiveness.
cards.explain: Monitoring continues throughout the project through risk reviews and audits, and often leads to updating the register, closing outdated risks, or activating contingency plans.

cards.back: The combined effect of uncertainty on the project as a whole, beyond individual risks.
cards.explain: Overall risk reflects variability in the total project outcome, often assessed with Monte Carlo simulation, and is reported in the risk report rather than the register.

cards.back: A hierarchical categorization of risk sources.
cards.explain: It shares the RBS acronym with the resource breakdown structure and serves as a prompt list during risk identification, grouping risks by source like technical or external.

cards.topic: Change control, issues, and corrective action
cards.back: A formal proposal to modify a deliverable, baseline, document, or other project element.
cards.explain: Corrective actions, preventive actions, defect repairs, and updates all flow as change requests into integrated change control before any baseline is touched.

cards.topic: Change control, issues, and corrective action
cards.back: Reviewing, approving, rejecting, and managing changes across project objectives and plans.
cards.explain: In predictive scenarios the PM first analyzes impact, then submits the request to the CCB or other authority rather than approving or implementing it alone.

cards.topic: Change control, issues, and corrective action
cards.back: A record of change requests and their status, decisions, and implementation details.
cards.explain: Tracks every change request, including rejected ones, while the issue log tracks current problems that need resolution.

cards.topic: Change control, issues, and corrective action
cards.back: The established procedure for submitting, evaluating, approving, and implementing changes.
cards.explain: Typical exam order is evaluate the impact, identify options, submit to the decision authority, then update plans and communicate once approved.

cards.topic: Change control, issues, and corrective action
cards.back: Controlling and documenting the functional and physical characteristics of products and deliverables.
cards.explain: Focuses on the product's specifications and versions, while change control focuses on changes to project baselines and plans.

cards.topic: Change control, issues, and corrective action
cards.back: An approved configuration used as a reference for subsequent changes.
cards.explain: Version control applies this idea, letting teams know exactly which approved version of a product or document is current before anything else changes.

cards.topic: Change control, issues, and corrective action
cards.back: An intentional activity to bring future project performance back into alignment with the plan.
cards.explain: Reacts to a variance that has already happened, like adding resources after falling behind schedule, while preventive action targets a predicted future problem.

cards.topic: Change control, issues, and corrective action
cards.back: An intentional activity designed to reduce the probability of future nonconformance.
cards.explain: Triggered by trends or warning signs before a variance appears, such as training a new team member before errors start occurring.

cards.topic: Change control, issues, and corrective action
cards.back: An activity to modify a nonconforming product or component.
cards.explain: Fixes the product itself, while corrective action adjusts project performance, so reworking a faulty component is defect repair rather than corrective action.

cards.topic: Change control, issues, and corrective action
cards.back: A document recording current issues, their owners, priorities, and resolution status.
cards.explain: Every entry needs an owner and due date, and it differs from the risk register, which tracks uncertain future events rather than current problems.

cards.topic: Change control, issues, and corrective action
cards.back: An obstacle that reduces a team's ability to perform work effectively.
cards.explain: Removing impediments is a core servant-leader duty of the Scrum Master, and they often surface during the Daily Scrum.

cards.topic: Change control, issues, and corrective action
cards.back: An obstacle that prevents a work item or activity from progressing.
cards.explain: Stops a specific item completely, whereas an impediment may merely slow the team, so blocked items are usually flagged visibly on the board.

cards.topic: Change control, issues, and corrective action
cards.back: Evaluating a proposed change or event's effects on scope, cost, schedule, quality, risk, and other areas.
cards.explain: It is the PM's first step when a change is requested, because decision makers need the effect on all constraints before approving or rejecting it.

cards.topic: Change control, issues, and corrective action
cards.back: Comparing actual results with planned or expected performance.
cards.explain: Answers how far off the project is and why, for example through cost or schedule variance, before deciding whether corrective action is needed.

cards.topic: Change control, issues, and corrective action
cards.back: Evaluating historical performance data to identify patterns and forecast future results.
cards.explain: Looks across several periods, such as CPI declining for three straight months, to predict where the project is heading rather than where it stands.

cards.topic: Change control, issues, and corrective action
cards.back: Addressing the underlying reason a problem occurred to reduce recurrence.
cards.explain: Fixing the symptom gets work moving today, but correcting the root cause, such as a flawed process, keeps the same problem from returning.

cards.topic: Change control, issues, and corrective action
cards.back: Documented authorization by a person or body with appropriate decision-making authority.
cards.explain: A hallway nod or agreement from someone lacking decision rights does not count, so the exam expects documented sign-off from the authorized approver.

cards.topic: Change control, issues, and corrective action
cards.back: Establishing an updated approved baseline following authorized changes.
cards.explain: Reserved for significant approved changes, since rebaselining just to hide poor performance would erase the variances stakeholders need to see.

cards.topic: Change control, issues, and corrective action
cards.back: A restriction on modifications during a defined period, often used to protect system stability.
cards.explain: Common before major releases or peak business periods, when typically only emergency changes are allowed through an expedited approval path.

cards.topic: Change control, issues, and corrective action
cards.back: An approach for controlling or supporting changes according to their nature, impact, and context.
cards.explain: Lets a project apply light control to low-impact changes and full board review to high-impact ones, tailoring governance instead of forcing one rigid process.

cards.back: Defines how goods and services will be acquired from outside the project organization.
cards.explain: Sets contract types, roles, the selection approach, and how procurements tie into schedule and risk, while each SOW describes the specific work a seller performs.

cards.back: Evaluating whether work should be performed internally or purchased externally.
cards.explain: Weighs cost alongside capability, capacity, intellectual property, and risk, and comes early because a buy decision triggers the whole procurement process.

cards.back: A description of the goods, services, or results a seller must provide.
cards.explain: It must be detailed enough for sellers to judge whether they can deliver, and it travels inside solicitation documents such as an RFP.

cards.back: A document seeking information about vendors, capabilities, or available solutions.
cards.explain: Use it first when the buyer does not yet know what solutions exist, since it gathers market information without requesting binding prices or proposals.

cards.back: A solicitation asking vendors to propose solutions, approaches, and pricing.
cards.explain: Choose it for complex or uncertain needs where sellers must propose how they would solve the problem, with selection weighing approach as well as price.

cards.back: A solicitation requesting price quotations for clearly specified goods or services.
cards.explain: Use it when the item is well defined and price is the main decision factor, such as buying a standard server configuration.

cards.back: A formal invitation for sellers to submit competitive bids, generally against well-defined specifications.
cards.explain: Much like an RFQ, it fits fully defined specifications where selection is typically based on the lowest responsive price, common in public sector buying.

cards.back: An agreement where the seller provides defined work for an agreed price.
cards.explain: Places most cost risk on the seller, so it fits well-defined scope, because vague scope leads sellers to pad prices or end up in disputes.

cards.back: A fixed-price contract in which the price generally does not change unless authorized changes occur.
cards.explain: The most common and lowest-risk contract for the buyer, with the seller absorbing any cost overruns unless the buyer changes the scope.

cards.back: A fixed-price contract allowing financial incentives based on agreed performance measures.
cards.explain: Includes a target cost, share ratio, and ceiling price, with the seller absorbing all costs above the ceiling, so the incentive rewards efficient performance.

cards.front: Fixed Price with Economic Price Adjustment (FPEPA)
cards.back: A fixed-price contract permitting defined adjustments for changes in economic conditions.
cards.explain: Fits multiyear contracts exposed to inflation or commodity swings, with adjustments tied to a published index such as fuel or steel prices.

cards.back: An agreement where the buyer reimburses allowable costs and typically pays an additional fee.
cards.explain: Places more cost risk on the buyer, so it suits uncertain or evolving scope, such as research work, where fixed pricing would be unrealistic.

cards.back: A cost-reimbursable contract paying allowable costs plus a fixed fee.
cards.explain: The fee is set from estimated costs and stays the same regardless of actual costs, so the seller earns nothing extra from overruns unless scope changes.

cards.back: A cost-reimbursable contract incorporating incentives for meeting agreed targets.
cards.explain: A share ratio splits savings or overruns against the target cost between buyer and seller, raising or lowering the seller's fee accordingly.

cards.back: A cost-reimbursable contract with an award fee based on the buyer's evaluation of performance.
cards.explain: The award depends largely on the buyer's subjective judgment and is generally not subject to appeal, unlike formula-based incentive fees.

cards.back: A contract using agreed labor rates and material costs, often combining features of fixed-price and cost-reimbursable arrangements.
cards.explain: Common for staff augmentation or small, undefined work, and buyers often add a not-to-exceed cap to control its open-ended cost risk.

cards.back: The distribution of financial and performance risk between buyer and seller.
cards.explain: Risk shifts toward the seller as contracts move from cost-plus to fixed price, so choosing a contract type is itself a risk transfer decision.

cards.back: Standards used to evaluate potential vendors and select a seller.
cards.explain: Defined before proposals arrive and often weighted, they may include technical approach, past performance, and financial capacity, not just price.

cards.back: A meeting where prospective sellers receive clarification about procurement requirements.
cards.explain: All prospective sellers get the same answers at the same time to keep the process fair, so private side meetings with one vendor are wrong.

cards.back: The process of reaching agreement on price, scope, responsibilities, terms, and conditions.
cards.explain: Happens before signing to clarify terms, with the PM supporting while the procurement or contracting authority usually holds signing authority.

cards.back: An agreement defining measurable service expectations and performance standards.
cards.explain: Common in operations and outsourcing, it sets measurable targets such as a four-hour response time and often defines penalties or credits when they are missed.

cards.back: Managing supplier obligations, performance, payments, modifications, and claims.
cards.explain: If a seller underperforms, the exam usually expects the PM to review the contract terms and follow the agreed process rather than terminating immediately.

cards.back: A review of procurement processes and results to identify compliance and improvement opportunities.
cards.explain: Reviews how the procurement process itself performed from planning through administration, and its lessons feed organizational process assets for future contracts.

cards.back: A request or assertion by a contracting party seeking compensation, adjustment, or contractual relief.
cards.explain: Contested changes become claims, and PMI prefers resolving them through negotiation first, using alternative dispute resolution such as mediation or arbitration only if needed.

cards.back: Confirming contractual obligations have been fulfilled and completing required administrative actions.
cards.explain: Usually completes before project closure and includes resolving open claims, confirming deliverable acceptance, and making final payment.

cards.back: Technology that performs tasks requiring capabilities such as prediction, pattern recognition, reasoning, or content generation.
cards.explain: On the exam AI is treated as a tool that augments the PM, such as forecasting or summarizing, while humans keep accountability for decisions.

cards.back: AI that produces new text, images, code, or other content based on learned patterns.
cards.explain: Generative AI drafts content like status reports or meeting summaries, but outputs must be reviewed for accuracy because it can produce convincing falsehoods.

cards.back: Methods enabling systems to identify patterns and improve predictions or decisions using data.
cards.explain: Machine learning powers predictive analytics, such as learning from past projects to flag tasks likely to slip, and its quality depends heavily on training data.

cards.back: Using historical and current data to forecast possible future results.
cards.explain: It forecasts what is likely to happen, such as schedule overruns, while generative AI creates new content, and both depend on good-quality data.

cards.back: An AI-generated output that presents fabricated or incorrect information as though it were accurate.
cards.explain: The remedy is human verification before use, so a PM fact-checks AI-generated summaries, estimates, or contract language rather than trusting fluent output.

cards.back: An approach requiring human involvement in reviewing, guiding, or approving AI-supported decisions.
cards.explain: Exam answers favor keeping a person responsible for reviewing and approving AI outputs, especially for high-impact decisions affecting people, contracts, or compliance.

cards.back: Policies, controls, and accountability structures governing responsible AI use.
cards.explain: Governance sets the organizational rules, such as approved tools and data-handling policies, which a PM must follow before using AI on project data.

cards.back: Systematic errors or unfair outcomes arising from data, models, or their application.
cards.explain: Skewed training data can produce unfair outputs, such as resource recommendations favoring certain groups, so outputs need monitoring and data should be representative.

cards.back: Appropriate protection and use of personal or sensitive information.
cards.explain: A PM should never paste confidential or personal stakeholder data into public AI tools without approval, as privacy laws and organizational policies may prohibit it.

cards.back: Policies and responsibilities for managing data quality, security, access, and use.
cards.explain: Data governance covers ownership, quality, and access across the whole data lifecycle, while data privacy is narrower, focusing on protecting personal or sensitive information.

cards.back: Developing and using AI in ways that emphasize reliability, accountability, fairness, safety, and transparency.
cards.explain: Responsible AI is the set of principles while AI governance is the structure enforcing them, and transparency means stakeholders know when and how AI was used.

cards.back: Meeting current needs while considering long-term environmental, social, and economic consequences.
cards.explain: PMBOK 8 makes integrating sustainability a principle, so PMs weigh long-term environmental, social, and economic effects of decisions, not just immediate project cost.

cards.back: A framework for evaluating environmental impacts, social responsibilities, and governance practices.
cards.explain: ESG is how investors and organizations measure responsible conduct, so projects increasingly report against criteria such as emissions, labor practices, and board oversight.

cards.back: An evaluation of performance across people, planet, and profit.
cards.explain: Remember people, planet, profit: a project can be profitable yet fail the triple bottom line if it harms communities or the environment.

cards.back: The greenhouse gas emissions associated with an activity, product, organization, or project.
cards.explain: A PM can reduce it through choices like virtual meetings instead of travel or lower-emission suppliers, and it is usually reported as CO2 equivalent.

cards.back: Evaluating environmental impacts across the stages of a product's life.
cards.explain: LCA spans cradle to grave, from raw materials through disposal, unlike life cycle costing, which totals financial costs rather than environmental impacts.

cards.back: Adhering to applicable laws, regulations, and mandatory requirements.
cards.explain: Regulations are mandatory, unlike many voluntary standards, so compliance requirements act as fixed constraints that cannot be traded away to save schedule or cost.

cards.back: A structured assessment of adherence to applicable rules, standards, policies, and obligations.
cards.explain: Like a quality audit, it is an independent check of conformance, and its findings drive corrective actions and process improvements.

cards.back: Preparing, supporting, and helping people adopt changes to processes, technology, or ways of working.
cards.explain: Projects deliver outputs but benefits appear only when people adopt them, so OCM activities like communication, training, and reinforcement are planned alongside technical work.

cards.back: Evaluating whether an organization or group is prepared to implement and adopt a change.
cards.explain: Done before rollout, it reveals gaps in awareness, skills, or leadership support so the PM can plan training and communication before deployment.

cards.back: Opposition, reluctance, or barriers affecting the adoption of a proposed change.
cards.explain: Treat resistance as information: engage resisters, understand their concerns, and address root causes like fear of job loss rather than forcing adoption.

cards.back: A change management model consisting of Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, and Reinforcement.
cards.explain: Use it to diagnose where people are stuck, so staff who know the new system but lack ability need practice and support, not more awareness emails.

cards.back: Evaluating Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, and Environmental factors.
cards.explain: PESTLE scans only external macro-environment factors, helping identify risks and enterprise environmental factors, while SWOT also covers internal strengths and weaknesses.

cards.back: Identifying Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats.
cards.explain: Strengths and weaknesses are internal while opportunities and threats are external, and SWOT is a common technique for identifying project risks.

cards.back: Volatility, Uncertainty, Complexity, and Ambiguity; characteristics of challenging environments.
cards.explain: High-VUCA environments favor adaptive approaches, short feedback loops, and resilience, since detailed upfront plans quickly become obsolete.

cards.back: Maintaining essential business functions during and after a disruption.
cards.explain: Business continuity keeps critical operations running during a disruption, while disaster recovery restores systems afterward and is one component of a continuity plan.

cards.back: Restoring critical systems, data, or operations following a significant disruption.
cards.explain: Measured by recovery time and recovery point objectives, it brings IT systems and data back, whereas business continuity keeps the whole business operating.

cards.back: Formally completing or terminating a project and finalizing its activities.
cards.explain: Closure applies whether a project finishes or is cancelled early; either way the PM documents status, releases resources, and archives records and lessons learned.

cards.back: Completing final records, reports, approvals, and organizational requirements.
cards.explain: Administrative closure is internal housekeeping like archiving files and releasing resources, while contract closure settles agreements with sellers and normally happens first.

cards.back: Documented confirmation that deliverables meet agreed acceptance requirements.
cards.explain: Formal acceptance is the output of validating scope with the customer or sponsor, and it is needed before the project can be formally closed.

cards.back: Transferring completed deliverables and responsibilities to the group that will operate or maintain them.
cards.explain: Transition is planned early, with transition requirements like training and support documentation, so benefits can continue after the project team disbands.

cards.back: Confirmation that people, processes, technology, and support arrangements are prepared to sustain the solution.
cards.explain: Assess operational readiness before go-live, because deploying when support staff, processes, or tools are not ready puts the intended benefits at risk.

cards.back: A summary of performance, outcomes, significant changes, lessons learned, and closure information.
cards.explain: Unlike periodic status reports, the final report is issued once at closure and compares achieved scope, schedule, cost, quality, and benefits against objectives.

cards.back: A record of lessons identified throughout the project.
cards.explain: The register is a project document updated throughout the project, and at closure its contents are transferred to the organizational lessons learned repository.

cards.back: An organizational collection of historical experiences and improvement recommendations.
cards.explain: The repository is an organizational process asset that future projects consult during planning, so it outlives any single project's register.

cards.back: Capturing, organizing, sharing, and applying organizational knowledge.
cards.explain: Knowledge management covers explicit knowledge in documents and tacit knowledge in people's heads, which spreads through conversations, mentoring, and communities of practice.

cards.back: A collaborative review used to identify improvements based on recent work.
cards.explain: Retrospectives inspect how the team works, including process, tools, and relationships, while a sprint review inspects the product increment with stakeholders.

cards.back: The formal transfer of deliverables, documentation, knowledge, and responsibilities.
cards.explain: A good handover includes training and documentation for the receiving team and usually requires their sign-off confirming they accept ownership.

cards.back: An evaluation after implementation to determine performance, adoption, and achievement of intended outcomes.
cards.explain: Conducted weeks or months after go-live, the review checks whether intended outcomes and benefits are actually occurring, unlike a retrospective focused on team process.

cards.topic: PMBOK 8th Edition principles and performance domains
cards.back: Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring and Controlling, Closing: the five focus areas that organize PMBOK 8's processes.
cards.explain: Focus areas are not project phases; they can repeat within every phase or iteration, much as process groups did in earlier PMBOK editions.

cards.back: EV − AC
cards.explain: Negative means over budget, so EV of $40,000 minus AC of $50,000 gives a CV of negative $10,000, meaning more was spent than value earned.
cards.note: Positive = under budget

cards.back: EV − PV
cards.explain: Negative means behind schedule in value terms, and it always returns to zero at completion, which is why it loses meaning late in a project.
cards.note: Positive = ahead of schedule (in earned-value terms)

cards.back: EV ÷ AC
cards.explain: Above 1 means under budget and below 1 means over budget; in CV, SV, CPI and SPI, EV always comes first, which prevents sign errors.
cards.note: Above 1 = favorable; 0.80 = earning $0.80 of value per $1 spent

cards.back: EV ÷ PV
cards.explain: Below 1 means behind schedule, but because it compares value rather than time, it drifts back toward 1 near project end even if the project is late.
cards.note: Above 1 = favorable; 0.80 = 80% of planned value earned (not calendar delay)

cards.back: BAC ÷ CPI
cards.explain: Use this variant when the scenario says current cost performance is expected to continue, the most common exam assumption when nothing else is specified.
cards.note: Forecast cost if current cost efficiency continues

cards.front: EAC, original estimate for remaining work
cards.back: AC + (BAC − EV)
cards.explain: Use it when the variance was a one-time, atypical event and the rest of the work is expected to go as originally budgeted.
cards.note: Forecast if remaining work runs at the original budgeted rates

cards.back: EAC − AC
cards.explain: ETC is the money still needed from today, while EAC is the total including what was already spent, so ETC plus AC equals EAC.
cards.note: Remaining estimated cost

cards.back: BAC − EAC
cards.explain: Positive means the project is forecast to finish under budget and negative means over, because it compares the budget against the EAC forecast rather than current actuals.
cards.note: Positive = favorable

cards.back: (BAC − EV) ÷ (BAC − AC)
cards.explain: Above 1 means remaining work must be done more efficiently than planned to stay on budget, so a high TCPI signals the target may be unrealistic.
cards.note: Cost efficiency needed on remaining work to finish on budget

cards.explain: It weights the most likely value four times, pulling the result toward the realistic estimate, so use it when the question says PERT or beta distribution.
cards.note: Weighted three-point estimate

cards.explain: Use it when the question says triangular or simple average, since it weights extremes more than PERT and results differ when estimates are skewed.
cards.note: Equal-weight three-point estimate

cards.explain: A wider gap between pessimistic and optimistic means more uncertainty, and roughly 68% of outcomes fall within one standard deviation of the PERT mean.
cards.note: Size of the estimate's uncertainty

cards.explain: Exam questions often ask how many channels are added, so compute the before and after totals and subtract, remembering to count the PM in n.
cards.note: Possible pairwise channels among n people

cards.back: Probability × Impact
cards.explain: Use negative impacts for threats and positive for opportunities, so a 40% chance of a $5,000 opportunity contributes positive $2,000 to the total.
cards.note: Probability-weighted impact of a risk

cards.back: (Benefit − Cost) ÷ Cost × 100%
cards.explain: Higher ROI is better, but unlike NPV it ignores the time value of money, so prefer NPV when the timing of cash flows matters.
cards.note: Return as a percentage of cost

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.back: Risk is uncertain (future); an issue is happening now
cards.explain: Memory hook: a risk might happen, an issue did happen; when a risk materializes, the PM executes the planned response and records it in the issue log.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.back: QA focuses on processes; QC checks deliverable results
cards.explain: QA asks whether the team is following the right process, QC asks whether this deliverable is correct; audits signal QA, while testing signals QC.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.back: Formal stakeholder acceptance vs. checking deliverables are correct
cards.explain: Order matters: QC checks correctness internally first, then Validate Scope seeks the customer's formal acceptance, so correct deliverables can still be rejected.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.back: Sponsor authorizes and champions; the PM manages delivery
cards.explain: If a decision needs money, strategic priority, or authority beyond the plan, it goes to the sponsor; if it is about delivering the plan, the PM owns it.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.back: Maximizes product value vs. makes Scrum effective
cards.explain: The product owner decides what gets built and in what order, while the Scrum Master coaches the team and removes impediments but never sets priorities.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.back: Inspects the product/outcome vs. improves how the team works
cards.explain: The review looks at what was built with stakeholders invited, while the retrospective looks at how the Scrum Team worked and comes after the review.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.back: Allowance for identified risks vs. for unforeseen work
cards.explain: Contingency covers known unknowns and is within the PM's control, while management reserve covers unknown unknowns and requires management approval to use.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.back: Add resources/cost vs. overlap activities
cards.explain: Crashing costs money while fast tracking adds risk and possible rework, and both only shorten the schedule when applied to critical path activities.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.back: May change the finish date vs. stays within float
cards.explain: Leveling resolves overallocation even if the critical path moves, while smoothing protects the end date and so may not resolve every resource conflict.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.back: Fixes a performance deviation vs. reduces future problems
cards.explain: Corrective action responds to something already off track, like recovering a late milestone, while preventive action acts on a trend before it becomes a variance.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.back: Usable product for learning vs. exploratory model
cards.explain: An MVP is a real, usable product released to users for feedback, while a prototype may be a throwaway mockup never used in production.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.back: Request-to-delivery vs. start-to-completion
cards.explain: Lead time is what the customer experiences, including waiting in the backlog, while cycle time is what the team controls once work actually begins.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.back: Improve what exists repeatedly vs. add completed portions
cards.explain: Iterative is like repeatedly refining a sketch of a whole painting, while incremental is like finishing one room of a house at a time; agile combines both.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.front: Scope Creep vs. Approved Scope Change
cards.back: Uncontrolled expansion vs. controlled modification
cards.explain: The difference is approval: any scope addition that skips change control is creep, even when the customer asked for it.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.back: Excludes vs. includes management reserve
cards.explain: Budget equals the cost baseline plus management reserve, and contingency sits inside the baseline, which is why earned value is measured against the baseline.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.back: Reduce the threat vs. eliminate exposure to it
cards.explain: Avoidance changes the plan so the threat cannot occur, like dropping a risky feature, while mitigation keeps the activity but lowers probability or impact.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.back: Understand the problem, its cause, its impact and the stakeholders involved before choosing a response.
cards.explain: On the exam, eliminate answers that jump straight to escalating, replacing people, or changing plans before the PM has gathered facts and analyzed impact.
cards.situation: A team member reports a sudden spike in defects and the sponsor wants an immediate fix.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.back: When the team has the authority and capability to resolve an issue, work it out together before raising it to the sponsor.
cards.explain: PMI wants problems solved at the lowest effective level first, escalating to the sponsor only when authority, thresholds, or team capability are exceeded.
cards.situation: Two developers disagree on a design choice that is within the team's authority.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.back: Use formal change control for predictive baselines; agile backlog reprioritization follows the product's own governance.
cards.explain: In a predictive project, route baseline changes through integrated change control, while in agile the product owner can reorder the backlog without a change request.
cards.situation: A stakeholder asks to add a feature to a project with an approved scope baseline.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.back: Check that the work still supports the business case and intended outcomes, not only that scope is delivered.
cards.explain: Delivering every planned feature is not success if the business need has changed, so PMI favors answers that revisit value and adjust scope.
cards.situation: A market shift means a planned feature may no longer deliver the expected benefit.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.back: Address the underlying cause rather than repeatedly treating symptoms.
cards.explain: Repeated workarounds signal an unaddressed cause, so PMI favors root cause analysis and corrective action that stops the problem from recurring.
cards.situation: The same integration error keeps returning after each quick patch.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.back: Support team autonomy while keeping accountability and appropriate governance.
cards.explain: Let the team decide how to do the work, but keep clear roles, decision rights, and reporting so that autonomy never means lack of oversight.
cards.situation: A self-organizing team wants to change how it plans its sprints.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.front: Match the response to risk or issue
cards.back: Use risk responses for uncertainty; use issue resolution for problems already happening.
cards.explain: If the event has not occurred, update the risk register and plan responses; if it already occurred, use the issue log and act now.
cards.situation: A supplier has already missed a delivery date that the schedule depends on.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.back: Schedule pressure never automatically justifies bypassing standards.
cards.explain: PMI answers never skip testing, safety checks, or regulatory steps to save time; instead, negotiate scope, schedule, or resources through proper channels.
cards.situation: The sponsor suggests skipping a required safety test to hit the launch date.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.back: Keep stakeholders involved throughout the project, not only when you need their approval.
cards.explain: Ongoing engagement surfaces concerns early and builds trust, so answers that involve stakeholders only at sign-off or after problems arise are usually wrong.
cards.situation: A key user group has not been contacted since requirements sign-off months ago.

cards.theme: PMI decision rules and confused pairs
cards.back: The best answer depends on whether the environment is predictive, agile or hybrid.
cards.explain: Read the scenario for clues like sprints, a backlog, or a fixed scope baseline, then choose the response that fits that delivery approach.
cards.situation: A project has fixed regulatory deliverables plus a customer app with changing requirements.

cards.topic: Develop an integrated project management plan and plan delivery
cards.front: Assess project needs, complexity, and magnitude
cards.back: Before picking an approach or reusing an old plan, assess needs, complexity, magnitude, constraints, and context so planning fits this project.
cards.explain: Before picking an approach or reusing an old plan, assess needs, complexity, magnitude, constraints, and context so planning fits this project.
cards.note: Assess needs, complexity, magnitude, and constraints before committing.
traps: Reuse a prior plan because scope looks similar
Choose a familiar approach before assessing complexity
Judge complexity by budget size alone

quick_qs.prompt: What should come before selecting a delivery approach for a new project?

options.A: Copying the plan from the most similar past project
options.B: Assessing needs, complexity, magnitude, and context
options.C: Agreeing a fixed delivery date with the sponsor
options.D: Asking the vendor to estimate from a feature list

quick_qs.why: Approach and plan depth should follow from an assessment of this project's needs and complexity, not from habit or pressure.

quick_qs.prompt: Which measure alone does NOT define project complexity?

options.A: Budget size
options.B: Number of interacting stakeholders
options.C: Regulatory and integration constraints
options.D: Uncertainty in requirements

quick_qs.why: Complexity comes from interactions, constraints, and uncertainty. A large or small budget says little about how complex the work is.

cards.topic: Develop an integrated project management plan and plan delivery
cards.front: Create an integrated project management plan
cards.back: Combine all workstream plans into one integrated plan so dependencies, conflicts, and shared decisions across scope, schedule, cost, and risk surface before execution.
cards.explain: Combine all workstream plans into one integrated plan so dependencies, conflicts, and shared decisions across scope, schedule, cost, and risk surface before execution.
cards.note: Integrate workstream plans into one plan before execution starts.
traps: Keep separate plans and reconcile during execution
Have functional managers approve only their own plans
Start delivery before plans are integrated

quick_qs.prompt: Workstream plans show conflicting milestone dates before kickoff. Best response?

options.A: Let each workstream keep its dates and reconcile later
options.B: Have each functional manager approve their own plan
options.C: Start execution and resolve conflicts as they arise
options.D: Integrate the plans so dependencies and dates align

quick_qs.why: An integrated plan exposes cross-workstream dependencies and conflicts before they turn into delivery problems.

quick_qs.prompt: What is the main purpose of an integrated project management plan?

options.A: Coordinate components and decisions project-wide
options.B: Give each department control of its own baseline
options.C: Record the sign-off of every functional manager
options.D: Replace stakeholder input with one master schedule

quick_qs.why: Integration connects scope, schedule, cost, and risk so decisions in one area account for the others.

cards.topic: Develop an integrated project management plan and plan delivery
cards.front: Collect and analyze data to make informed project decisions
cards.back: Make decisions from collected and analyzed project data, not opinion or siloed readings, and act on good-enough data rather than waiting for perfect metrics.
cards.explain: Make decisions from collected and analyzed project data, not opinion or siloed readings, and act on good-enough data rather than waiting for perfect metrics.
cards.note: Collect and analyze project data, then decide.
traps: Defer to senior opinion when data is incomplete
Let each team interpret its own data separately
Wait until every metric is fully mature

quick_qs.prompt: Pilot metrics are mixed. What should guide the decision to scale?

options.A: Senior stakeholders' opinion of the pilot
options.B: Each team's separate reading of its own data
options.C: Analysis of the combined pilot data
options.D: Waiting until every metric fully matures

quick_qs.why: Shared analysis of the data gives an informed, consistent basis for the decision. Opinion and siloed readings do not.

quick_qs.prompt: Why is waiting for complete, perfect data a poor choice?

options.A: It delays action that is needed now
options.B: It overloads the team with extra reporting
options.C: It breaks the change control process rules
options.D: It makes expert opinion less reliable later

quick_qs.why: Projects decide under uncertainty. Waiting for perfect data can stall necessary action.

cards.front: Identify value components with key stakeholders
cards.back: Define what value means with all key stakeholders before prioritizing work, so delivery reflects every important value dimension, not one viewpoint.
cards.explain: Define what value means with all key stakeholders before prioritizing work, so delivery reflects every important value dimension, not one viewpoint.
cards.note: Identify value components with key stakeholders before prioritizing.
traps: Treat the business case as the only value definition
Let the sponsor rank value without others' input
Prioritize first and define value during delivery

quick_qs.prompt: When should value components be identified with stakeholders?

options.A: After the first release ships
options.B: During closure and benefit review
options.C: Once the backlog is fully estimated
options.D: Before work is prioritized

quick_qs.why: Value definitions are the basis for prioritization. Defining them later can send delivery in the wrong direction.

quick_qs.prompt: Why isn't the business case alone enough to define project value?

options.A: It is written before the charter is approved
options.B: It only lists costs, never expected benefits
options.C: It may miss value other groups care about
options.D: It is owned by finance instead of the sponsor

quick_qs.why: The business case may not capture operational, customer, or user value, so stakeholders need to be engaged.

cards.front: Verify a measurement system is in place to track benefits
cards.back: Confirm early that benefit metrics, baselines, data sources, and owners exist, because milestones and features delivered do not prove benefits are realized.
cards.explain: Confirm early that benefit metrics, baselines, data sources, and owners exist, because milestones and features delivered do not prove benefits are realized.
cards.note: Verify benefit metrics, baselines, data sources, and owners exist.
traps: Treat milestones or features as benefit measures
Leave benefit measurement until after handover
Ask for benefit descriptions only at closure

quick_qs.prompt: A dashboard tracks installation progress only. What is missing for benefits?

options.A: More detailed milestone dates per site
options.B: A bigger contingency reserve for rework
options.C: Weekly status meetings with the vendor
options.D: Outcome metrics, baselines, and owners

quick_qs.why: Progress shows output. Benefits need outcome measures with baselines, data sources, and someone accountable for reporting.

quick_qs.prompt: When should the benefits measurement system be verified?

options.A: During planning, before go-live
options.B: After operations accepts delivery
options.C: Only at final project closure
options.D: When the sponsor asks for a report

quick_qs.why: Verifying measurement early ensures baselines exist and outcomes can be tracked from the start.

cards.back: Plan procurement early from scope, requirements, risks, and sourcing constraints, defining criteria, timing, and responsibilities before engaging vendors.
cards.explain: Plan procurement early from scope, requirements, risks, and sourcing constraints, defining criteria, timing, and responsibilities before engaging vendors.
cards.note: Plan procurement from scope, requirements, risks, and constraints.
traps: Issue purchase orders fast without planning
Default to the preferred or cheapest supplier
Wait until design is complete to plan sourcing

quick_qs.prompt: What should procurement planning be based on?

options.A: The organization's preferred supplier list
options.B: Procurement steps proposed by vendors
options.C: The lowest price quoted by any supplier
options.D: Scope, needs, risks, and constraints

quick_qs.why: Sourcing decisions must fit project-specific needs and risks. Supplier habits and price alone may not.

quick_qs.prompt: Why is delaying procurement planning until design is final risky?

options.A: Lead times and sourcing limits hit the schedule
options.B: Vendors cannot bid once the design is finished
options.C: Contracts cannot change after design is approved
options.D: Design documents legally replace the SOW

quick_qs.why: Late planning leaves no room for supplier lead times, licensing, or capacity limits, which creates schedule risk.

cards.front: Verify objectives of the procurement agreement are met
cards.back: Before closing a procurement, verify deliverables against contract terms and acceptance criteria; invoices or vendor claims do not prove objectives were met.
cards.explain: Before closing a procurement, verify deliverables against contract terms and acceptance criteria; invoices or vendor claims do not prove objectives were met.
cards.note: Verify deliverables against contract and acceptance criteria before closing.
traps: Close because all items and invoices arrived
Accept based on vendor confirmation alone
Defer verification until operations finds problems

quick_qs.prompt: What shows that a procurement's objectives were met?

options.A: Every invoice received and paid
options.B: Checks against the contract's criteria
options.C: A written completion notice from the vendor
options.D: No complaints from operations so far

quick_qs.why: Only buyer-side verification against contracted terms and acceptance criteria confirms objectives were achieved.

quick_qs.prompt: Equipment is delivered but user acceptance testing is not done. What next?

options.A: Close the contract since delivery is complete
options.B: Accept based on the vendor's own test results
options.C: Close now and let operations log any defects
options.D: Finish acceptance checks before closure

quick_qs.why: Closing before acceptance shifts unresolved risk to operations and weakens the buyer's position.

cards.front: Plan and manage the procurement strategy
cards.back: Manage one procurement strategy aligned to delivery needs, risks, and constraints instead of fragmented, rushed, or default sourcing decisions.
cards.explain: Manage one procurement strategy aligned to delivery needs, risks, and constraints instead of fragmented, rushed, or default sourcing decisions.
cards.note: Align the procurement strategy to overall delivery needs and risks.
traps: Let each team choose its own suppliers
Buy as soon as funding becomes available
Use preferred or cheapest vendors without review

quick_qs.prompt: Several teams want to source their vendors separately. What is the main risk?

options.A: Higher attendance at bidder conferences
options.B: Fragmented contracts and accountability
options.C: Too few change requests during delivery
options.D: Contracts that close faster than planned

quick_qs.why: Separate sourcing splits contracts and accountability and can conflict with the overall delivery strategy.

quick_qs.prompt: What should a procurement strategy cover?

options.A: Only the supplier offering the lowest price
options.B: Purchase timing tied to each funding release
options.C: Sourcing, risk, and fit with delivery needs
options.D: Vendor choices made by each workstream lead

quick_qs.why: The strategy coordinates sourcing with delivery needs and risks across the whole project.

cards.front: Plan spend tracking throughout the project life cycle
cards.back: Plan how spending is tracked and reported across the life cycle so variances and trends are caught early enough to act, not at closure.
cards.explain: Plan how spending is tracked and reported across the life cycle so variances and trends are caught early enough to act, not at closure.
cards.note: Plan life-cycle spend tracking with a regular reporting cadence.
traps: Track spending only after budget is exceeded
Leave tracking to finance without project context
Review spending only at closure

quick_qs.prompt: Why is exception-only spend tracking weak?

options.A: It produces too many variance reports
options.B: It requires earned value on every task
options.C: It misses trends before overruns occur
options.D: It conflicts with the cost baseline format

quick_qs.why: Tracking only once limits are breached removes the early warning needed to correct course.

quick_qs.prompt: Who should interpret project cost variances?

options.A: Finance alone, once payments post
options.B: The vendor submitting the invoices
options.C: The PM and finance, in context
options.D: The sponsor at the closure review

quick_qs.why: Finance needs project context to explain variances; the PM supplies it during tracking, not after.

cards.back: Use reserves only under approved rules: contingency for identified risks via triggers, management reserve via governance, with documented, reforecast, auditable drawdowns.
cards.explain: Use reserves only under approved rules: contingency for identified risks via triggers, management reserve via governance, with documented, reforecast, auditable drawdowns.
cards.note: Tie every reserve use to triggers, rules, approval, and records.
traps: Use contingency for general overruns or scope additions
Draw management reserve without governance approval
Spend first and document or approve later

quick_qs.prompt: Who normally approves access to management reserve?

options.A: The project manager alone
options.B: Governance, e.g. the sponsor
options.C: The vendor's account manager
options.D: Each work package team lead

quick_qs.why: Using management reserve normally needs governance approval with documented impact and funding rationale; the PM cannot draw it alone.

quick_qs.prompt: A funded risk response is complete. What should happen to the reserve?

options.A: Return all unused reserve automatically
options.B: Keep the original reserve forecast as is
options.C: Spend what is left on quality improvements
options.D: Reforecast it against remaining risk

quick_qs.why: After a response runs, reserves and assumptions are reforecast against current exposure before any release or change.

cards.topic: Plan and optimize quality of products/deliverables
cards.back: Identify applicable regulations with experts, build their requirements and evidence into quality controls, and close compliance gaps before acceptance or release.
cards.explain: Identify applicable regulations with experts, build their requirements and evidence into quality controls, and close compliance gaps before acceptance or release.
cards.note: Map regulations into quality controls and capture required evidence.
traps: Defer compliance checks to final audit or handover
Reuse an old checklist without tailoring
Escalate or seek exceptions before analyzing requirements

quick_qs.prompt: New regulatory guidance arrives mid-development. What should the PM do first?

options.A: Finish the release, then audit it
options.B: Assess it and update quality controls
options.C: Ask the sponsor to approve an exception
options.D: Reuse the last project's checklist

quick_qs.why: Compliance requirements must be analyzed and built into controls before more work proceeds, avoiding rework and approval delays.

quick_qs.prompt: When should compliance evidence be captured?

options.A: Only at operational handover
options.B: After auditors specifically ask for it
options.C: Through controls during delivery
options.D: When users begin reporting defects

quick_qs.why: Evidence built into controls during delivery supports audit and acceptance; collecting it late risks failed approvals.

cards.front: Prepare a schedule based on the selected development approach
cards.back: Match the schedule to the selected approach: dependency-based baselines for predictive, rolling-wave release forecasts for agile, and linked milestones and iterations for hybrid.
cards.explain: Match the schedule to the selected approach: dependency-based baselines for predictive, rolling-wave release forecasts for agile, and linked milestones and iterations for hybrid.
cards.note: Build the schedule model that fits the chosen development approach.
traps: Force a detailed Gantt chart onto uncertain agile scope
Defer scheduling until every date is confirmed
Combine task dates without validating dependencies

quick_qs.prompt: An agile team faces volatile scope. Which schedule view fits best?

options.A: A full Gantt chart baselined upfront
options.B: Vendor milestones without dependencies
options.C: No forecast until velocity stabilizes
options.D: Sprint plans plus release forecasts

quick_qs.why: Adaptive scheduling gives near-term commitments and flexible longer-range forecasts without pretending the backlog is fixed.

quick_qs.prompt: A hybrid project has fixed hardware milestones and iterative software. How to schedule?

options.A: Use one predictive schedule for everything
options.B: Keep separate plans with no shared links
options.C: Link milestones with iteration cycles
options.D: Plan software only after hardware is done

quick_qs.why: A hybrid schedule integrates predictive milestones with adaptive iterations and their shared readiness dependencies.
