quick_qs.why: Risk profiles shift; monitoring means reassessing exposure and redirecting responses to the current threat.

quick_qs.prompt: Penetration-test findings change weekly. How should the active risk response be managed?

options.A: Keep the original approved plan
options.B: Update it as new evidence arrives
options.C: Escalate each weekly finding first
options.D: Continue rollout during investigation

quick_qs.why: Risk control keeps responses aligned with current evidence rather than the plan approved earlier.

cards.front: Communicate the status of a risk impact on the project
cards.back: Tell stakeholders how a risk affects schedule, scope, readiness, and decisions, with responses and options, promptly and before they make dependent decisions.
cards.explain: Tell stakeholders how a risk affects schedule, scope, readiness, and decisions, with responses and options, promptly and before they make dependent decisions.
cards.note: Communicate the risk's project impact, responses, and decisions needed.
traps: Report metrics without explaining consequences
Wait for final confirmation before communicating
Let specialists brief without project context

quick_qs.prompt: Owners must approve a cutover after a failed rollback rehearsal. What should the PM do?

options.A: Explain its impact on timing and continuity
options.B: Approve, since the window is hard to reschedule
options.C: Wait for another rehearsal to confirm failure
options.D: Ask owners to accept rollback limits themselves

quick_qs.why: Stakeholders need the risk's project impact before approving; delay or acceptance without information is unsafe.

quick_qs.prompt: An effective risk status update to governance includes:

options.A: Schedule variance only, to avoid distraction
options.B: Technical detail from the specialists involved
options.C: Impact, responses, and decisions needed
options.D: External data without project consequences

quick_qs.why: Governance needs the risk's effect on the project, the planned responses, and what decision is required.

cards.back: Before planning engagement or governance changes, assess cultural norms such as autonomy, trust, transparency, and decision styles, so change approaches fit and resistance is understood.
cards.explain: Before planning engagement or governance changes, assess cultural norms such as autonomy, trust, transparency, and decision styles, so change approaches fit and resistance is understood.
cards.note: Assess cultural norms and concerns before planning change.
traps: Mandate or enforce the change through managers
Assume benefits will dissolve resistance
Wait for resistance before assessing culture

quick_qs.prompt: Users resist a standard process because they value local autonomy. What should the PM do first?

options.A: Have managers enforce the new standard process
options.B: Assess autonomy norms and trust concerns
options.C: Proceed; benefits will reduce resistance
options.D: Escalate the resistance to executives

quick_qs.why: Understanding cultural drivers first lets the PM tailor engagement instead of forcing or ignoring resistance.

quick_qs.prompt: Two sites react differently to transparency dashboards. What is the best rollout approach?

options.A: Use one rollout since features are identical
options.B: Require every site to share all problems
options.C: Escalate the low-transparency site first
options.D: Tailor engagement to each site's culture

quick_qs.why: Cultural differences change how a rollout lands; assessing and tailoring per site improves adoption.

cards.front: Continually review the external business environment for impacts on project scope/backlog
cards.back: Set recurring reviews of regulations, markets, standards, and other external changes so their impacts reach scope or backlog early, not after commitments.
cards.explain: Set recurring reviews of regulations, markets, standards, and other external changes so their impacts reach scope or backlog early, not after commitments.
cards.note: Review external changes regularly and adjust scope or backlog.
traps: Freeze scope because changes are not final
Rely on others to notify the project
Wait until changes take effect

quick_qs.prompt: Regulatory guidance keeps evolving during planning. What should the PM put in place?

options.A: A scope freeze until guidance becomes final
options.B: A single check just before final submission
options.C: Recurring reviews to catch impacts early
options.D: Escalation of each new notice to executives

quick_qs.why: Continual review detects external impacts while they are cheap to absorb, avoiding late scope surprises.

quick_qs.prompt: In agile delivery, where are external market changes best absorbed?

options.A: Backlog refinement and reprioritization
options.B: A change freeze until release completes
options.C: Sales adding features whenever customers ask
options.D: Quarterly surveys of external partners

quick_qs.why: Regularly reviewing market changes and adjusting priorities through refinement keeps the backlog relevant.

cards.topic: Develop an integrated project management plan and plan delivery
cards.back: Define which information decisions, compliance, and sustainability reporting actually need, agreed across stakeholders, before planning; not everything, not siloed, not copied.
cards.explain: Define which information decisions, compliance, and sustainability reporting actually need, agreed across stakeholders, before planning; not everything, not siloed, not copied.
cards.note: Define decision-critical information requirements with stakeholders early.
traps: Collect all available data just in case
Let each workstream define its own needs
Reuse status metrics from past projects

quick_qs.prompt: What should drive which information a project collects and reports?

options.A: Decision, compliance, and sustainability needs
options.B: Whatever data the project tools capture automatically
options.C: Metrics used on the last similar project
options.D: Each workstream lead's personal preferences

quick_qs.why: Critical information requirements focus planning on what decisions and obligations need, avoiding overload and reporting gaps.

quick_qs.prompt: Why is 'collect everything available' a poor information strategy?

options.A: It breaks most data privacy regulations
options.B: It always exceeds the approved budget
options.C: It prevents teams from using dashboards
options.D: It buries decisions in irrelevant data

quick_qs.why: Collecting everything overloads planning with irrelevant information instead of targeting what decisions require.

cards.topic: Develop an integrated project management plan and plan delivery
cards.front: Assess consolidated project plans for dependencies, gaps, and continued business value
cards.back: Review subsidiary plans together, not one at a time, to expose cross-workstream dependencies, gaps, and threats to business value before execution.
cards.explain: Review subsidiary plans together, not one at a time, to expose cross-workstream dependencies, gaps, and threats to business value before execution.
cards.note: Assess the integrated plan for dependencies, gaps, and value.
traps: Approve each workstream plan separately
Push dependency resolution to the sponsor
Start execution and fix gaps later

quick_qs.prompt: Each workstream plan looks complete alone. What reveals hidden cross-plan problems?

options.A: Owner sign-off on each individual plan
options.B: Sponsor review at the next governance meeting
options.C: An integrated review of all plans together
options.D: Tracking issues once execution starts

quick_qs.why: Separate approvals miss interfaces; a consolidated assessment exposes conflicting dates, dependencies, and gaps.

quick_qs.prompt: Besides dependencies and gaps, what must a consolidated plan review confirm?

options.A: Every team used the same template format
options.B: The plan still delivers business value
options.C: All vendor contracts have been signed
options.D: Named people are assigned to every task

quick_qs.why: Misaligned plans can delay benefits the business case depends on, so continued value is part of the check.

cards.front: Obtain stakeholder agreement on project scope
cards.back: Secure explicit agreement on scope, assumptions, exclusions, and acceptance across stakeholders before baselining; funding approval or piecemeal sign-off is not agreement.
cards.explain: Secure explicit agreement on scope, assumptions, exclusions, and acceptance across stakeholders before baselining; funding approval or piecemeal sign-off is not agreement.
cards.note: Facilitate agreement on scope, exclusions, assumptions, and acceptance.
traps: Treat sponsor funding approval as scope agreement
Have leads approve only their own deliverables
Settle scope disagreements during execution

quick_qs.prompt: Which most clearly shows stakeholders agree on scope?

options.A: The sponsor has approved the project budget
options.B: Shared sign-off on inclusions, exclusions, acceptance
options.C: Each functional lead signed off their own piece
options.D: Nobody has raised objections during status meetings so far

quick_qs.why: Agreement must cover boundaries and acceptance across stakeholders; budget approval or silence does not settle interpretations.

quick_qs.prompt: Two departments read scope exclusions differently. When should this be resolved?

options.A: Before the scope baseline is set
options.B: During execution as details emerge
options.C: At final acceptance testing
options.D: At the first change control board meeting

quick_qs.why: Unresolved ambiguity turns into rework and change disputes, so agreement belongs before baselining and execution.

cards.front: Assess opportunities to deliver value incrementally
cards.back: Look for usable parts of the solution that can be released early, so benefits start sooner, feedback arrives earlier, and big-bang risk drops.
cards.explain: Look for usable parts of the solution that can be released early, so benefits start sooner, feedback arrives earlier, and big-bang risk drops.
cards.note: Identify and release usable value increments early.
traps: Wait for the full solution before releasing
Sequence by technical complexity, not value
Bundle everything into one final delivery

quick_qs.prompt: What should decide which increment ships first?

options.A: Which feature carries the most technical risk
options.B: Which team happens to finish its work first
options.C: Which feature the vendor prefers to build
options.D: Which feature delivers usable value soonest

quick_qs.why: Business value, not technical difficulty or convenience, drives incremental sequencing so users benefit earlier.

quick_qs.prompt: Main benefit of incremental delivery over one big final release?

options.A: Lower total cost in every case
options.B: No need for formal change control later
options.C: Earlier benefits and earlier feedback
options.D: Fewer requirements to document

quick_qs.why: Incremental releases enable earlier benefits realization and learning; one large package delays validation and raises risk.

cards.front: Define and plan resources based on requirements
cards.back: Derive resource types, skills, quantities, and timing from requirements, constraints, and delivery approach before committing dates, not from habit or availability.
cards.explain: Derive resource types, skills, quantities, and timing from requirements, constraints, and delivery approach before committing dates, not from habit or availability.
cards.note: Define resource needs from requirements, constraints, and approach.
traps: Copy the previous project's staffing
Accept whoever functional managers have free
Wait for execution problems to reveal needs

quick_qs.prompt: What should resource planning be based on first?

options.A: Whichever staff are currently free in each department
options.B: The resource list from a similar past project
options.C: Requirements, constraints, and delivery approach
options.D: The sponsor's preferred team members

quick_qs.why: Needs come from what the work requires; available or past staffing may not match required skills or timing.

quick_qs.prompt: When should resource needs be defined relative to committing rollout dates?

options.A: After the first rollout wave
options.B: Before committing the dates
options.C: Once issues appear in execution
options.D: Only after the first budget review

quick_qs.why: Late resource planning creates avoidable capacity gaps and delivery risk, so define needs before date commitments.

cards.back: The buyer selects the contract type to match scope clarity, risk allocation, and needed incentives; ignoring uncertainty in a fixed price invites change disputes.
cards.explain: The buyer selects the contract type to match scope clarity, risk allocation, and needed incentives; ignoring uncertainty in a fixed price invites change disputes.
cards.note: Choose contract type by scope clarity, risk, and incentives.
traps: Use the standard contract for every supplier
Pick the type with least administrative effort
Let the vendor choose the contract type

quick_qs.prompt: Who should determine the contract type for a procurement?

options.A: The buyer, based on project risk
options.B: The seller, after reviewing the RFP
options.C: Legal, using the default template
options.D: Finance, based on lowest admin cost

quick_qs.why: Contract strategy belongs to the buyer and should reflect project risk, scope clarity, and incentives.

quick_qs.prompt: Scope will change after discovery. Why is a pure fixed-price contract risky?

options.A: Fixed price contracts cannot include any change clauses
options.B: It removes all cost risk from the buyer
options.C: It forbids any performance incentives
options.D: It invites disputes over changing scope

quick_qs.why: Fixed price assumes clear scope; when scope is uncertain, every change becomes a negotiation or dispute.

cards.back: Prepare a negotiation strategy before talks, built from buyer objectives, risks, and available alternatives, rather than improvising or borrowing old or vendor approaches.
cards.explain: Prepare a negotiation strategy before talks, built from buyer objectives, risks, and available alternatives, rather than improvising or borrowing old or vendor approaches.
cards.note: Set objectives, risks, and alternatives before negotiating.
traps: Improvise positions from vendor reactions
Let the vendor propose the approach
Reuse the last contract's strategy

quick_qs.prompt: Which three inputs shape a negotiation strategy?

options.A: Vendor reputation, price, and history
options.B: Past contracts, templates, and rates
options.C: Sponsor wishes, deadlines, and budget
options.D: Objectives, risks, and alternatives

quick_qs.why: A strategy reflecting objectives, risks, and alternatives protects buyer interests and leverage.

quick_qs.prompt: Why not start negotiating and adjust to the vendor's reactions?

options.A: It breaks most organizations' procurement policies
options.B: It wastes the vendor's time
options.C: It weakens leverage and alignment
options.D: It always raises the final price

quick_qs.why: Entering unprepared weakens leverage and alignment with project objectives.

cards.back: Build financial needs from scope, schedule, risks, and constraints with delivery input; a sponsor's budget target alone is not a financial-needs analysis.
cards.explain: Build financial needs from scope, schedule, risks, and constraints with delivery input; a sponsor's budget target alone is not a financial-needs analysis.
cards.note: Analyze funding needs from scope, schedule, risks, constraints.
traps: Adopt the sponsor's budget target as plan
Let finance estimate without delivery input
Wait until all requirements are approved

quick_qs.prompt: The sponsor gave a high-level budget. What shows whether it is enough?

options.A: Comparing it with similar past budgets
options.B: Analyzing needs from scope, schedule, and risks
options.C: Asking finance to confirm the figure
options.D: Waiting to see the first quarterly cost variance report

quick_qs.why: Only analysis from project drivers and constraints shows whether the target covers actual needs.

quick_qs.prompt: Why shouldn't finance estimate project costs alone?

options.A: They lack delivery input on real effort
options.B: Finance estimates are not auditable
options.C: Only the sponsor may set budgets
options.D: Finance always overestimates contingency

quick_qs.why: Realistic estimates need delivery knowledge of effort, scope, and risk that finance does not hold alone.

cards.back: Proactively analyze emerging financial exposures such as inflation, currency, cash flow, rates, and fees, update forecasts and reserves, and bring options to governance early.
cards.explain: Proactively analyze emerging financial exposures such as inflation, currency, cash flow, rates, and fees, update forecasts and reserves, and bring options to governance early.
cards.note: Forecast exposure, update reserves, and present options early.
traps: Wait for invoices to confirm the impact
Request more money before analyzing exposure
Push cost increases onto workstreams or vendors

quick_qs.prompt: Total budget is approved, but payment timing is tight. What is the concern?

quick_qs.why: Updating who decides and who provides input protects continuity and value decisions.

cards.topic: Develop an integrated project management plan and plan delivery
cards.back: Before detailed scheduling, recommend one execution strategy that integrates constraints, dependencies, value, and delivery risk so all workstreams deliver in a coordinated way.
cards.explain: Before detailed scheduling, recommend one execution strategy that integrates constraints, dependencies, value, and delivery risk so all workstreams deliver in a coordinated way.
cards.note: Recommend an integrated strategy covering constraints, value, and risks
traps: Starting with the fastest workstream plan available
Letting vendors define the overall execution strategy
Waiting until all detailed requirements are approved

quick_qs.prompt: What should an execution strategy integrate before detailed scheduling begins?

options.A: Constraints, dependencies, value, and delivery risks
options.B: The fastest plan available for each individual workstream
options.C: Whatever approach vendors propose after contract award
options.D: Only the requirements that are already formally approved

quick_qs.why: An integrated strategy guides coordinated delivery; speed-only plans ignore dependencies, vendor-led strategy fragments ownership, and waiting delays alignment.

quick_qs.prompt: Who should own the overall project execution strategy?

options.A: The vendor holding the largest contract
options.B: Each workstream lead for their own area
options.C: The project manager, with vendor input
options.D: The sponsor, after detailed scheduling ends

quick_qs.why: Vendors should inform but not own the strategy; the PM recommends one integrated approach across workstreams before detailed scheduling.

cards.topic: Develop an integrated project management plan and plan delivery
cards.front: Maintain the integrated project management plan
cards.back: Keep the integrated plan current as conditions change, updating all affected components together so scope, schedule, cost, risk, and value stay aligned.
cards.explain: Keep the integrated plan current as conditions change, updating all affected components together so scope, schedule, cost, risk, and value stay aligned.
cards.note: Update the integrated plan across all affected components
traps: Freezing the baseline plan despite changed conditions
Letting workstream leads update plans independently
Updating only the schedule because it is visible

quick_qs.prompt: A change affects testing sequence and support timing. Which plan components should be updated?

options.A: Only the schedule, because stakeholders see it most
options.B: All integrated components the change affects
options.C: None, to preserve baseline stability
options.D: Whatever each workstream lead decides locally

quick_qs.why: Schedule-only updates miss scope, cost, risk, and value impacts; maintaining the whole integrated plan keeps decisions aligned with change.

quick_qs.prompt: Why should the project manager avoid independent workstream plan updates?

options.A: They always slow down governance approval cycles
options.B: They require separate sponsor sign-off each time
options.C: They increase documentation cost for the PMO
options.D: They break integration across workstreams

quick_qs.why: Independent updates fragment the plan, so workstreams stop reflecting shared dependencies and decisions.

cards.back: Decompose approved scope into manageable deliverables and work packages before estimating or scheduling, so work can be planned, assigned, and controlled without hidden gaps.
cards.explain: Decompose approved scope into manageable deliverables and work packages before estimating or scheduling, so work can be planned, assigned, and controlled without hidden gaps.
cards.note: Decompose scope into deliverables and work packages first
traps: Keeping scope high level for team flexibility
Letting vendors own decomposition after contract signing
Scheduling before decomposing deliverables into work packages

quick_qs.prompt: What is the main risk of scheduling before decomposing scope?

options.A: Team members lose flexibility in execution
options.B: Vendors cannot submit accurate proposals
options.C: Missing work stays hidden from the plan
options.D: The sponsor must re-approve the charter

quick_qs.why: Scheduling before decomposition can hide missing work; breaking scope down first supports planning, accountability, and control.

quick_qs.prompt: When should approved scope be broken into work packages?

options.A: Before estimating and sequencing work
options.B: After the vendors have signed their contracts
options.C: Once the schedule baseline is approved
options.D: Only when estimates start to slip

quick_qs.why: Teams cannot estimate or sequence reliably from high-level scope, so decomposition comes before estimating and scheduling.

cards.front: Examine the business value throughout the project
cards.back: Reassess business value regularly during delivery and adjust remaining work when conditions change, because initial assumptions and task completion do not prove continuing value.
cards.explain: Reassess business value regularly during delivery and adjust remaining work when conditions change, because initial assumptions and task completion do not prove continuing value.
cards.note: Reexamine value evidence and adjust remaining delivery decisions
traps: Continuing the plan because value was defined initially
Confirming value only at final closure
Tracking task completion instead of reassessing value

quick_qs.prompt: When should a project examine whether planned work still delivers business value?

options.A: Only at final closure, with finance
options.B: Only when the sponsor requests it
options.C: Once, when the business case is approved
options.D: Regularly, throughout delivery

quick_qs.why: Initial value assumptions can become outdated, and final-only checks come too late to adjust delivery.

quick_qs.prompt: A pilot shows strong usage, but users say outputs are too generic. What does this show?

options.A: Business value is confirmed by usage
options.B: Usage alone does not prove value
options.C: The pilot should be escalated immediately
options.D: Users should wait for later releases

quick_qs.why: Value examination reviews outcomes and assumptions, not activity metrics; strong usage can coexist with weak value.

cards.front: Manage and optimize resource needs and availability
cards.back: When scarce resources conflict, analyze capacity, priorities, and constraints and reallocate for overall project value before adding people or escalating.
cards.explain: When scarce resources conflict, analyze capacity, priorities, and constraints and reallocate for overall project value before adding people or escalating.
cards.note: Rebalance scarce resources against capacity, priorities, and constraints
traps: Adding people to every delayed workstream
Letting each workstream keep resources until done
Escalating conflicts before structured resource analysis

quick_qs.prompt: Two workstreams need the same specialists in one week. What comes first?

options.A: Analyze capacity, priorities, and constraints
options.B: Add more people to both workstreams immediately
options.C: Let the first workstream keep the specialists
options.D: Escalate the conflict to executives for a ruling

quick_qs.why: Optimizing allocation balances capacity, priorities, and constraints; escalation before analysis is premature and local hoarding hurts overall performance.

quick_qs.prompt: Why is adding people to every delayed workstream a weak response?

options.A: It always violates the resource calendar
options.B: It requires a formal change request first
options.C: It raises coordination cost and inefficiency
options.D: It shifts accountability to functional managers

quick_qs.why: More people everywhere can increase coordination overhead without addressing priorities; optimize allocation instead.

cards.back: Evaluate vendors objectively against agreed measures, evidence, and contract terms during delivery, not on relationship, self-reports, or only at completion.
cards.explain: Evaluate vendors objectively against agreed measures, evidence, and contract terms during delivery, not on relationship, self-reports, or only at completion.
cards.note: Evaluate vendor against agreed measures, evidence, and contract terms
traps: Accepting vendor claims because the relationship is good
Escalating the vendor before reviewing performance evidence
Waiting until all contracted work is complete

quick_qs.prompt: What should vendor performance evaluation be based on?

options.A: The quality of the working relationship
options.B: Agreed measures, evidence, and contract terms
options.C: The vendor's own self-certification reports
options.D: Positive stakeholder feedback on demonstrations

quick_qs.why: Positive relationships, demos, and self-reports do not replace objective evidence against agreed measures and contract terms.

quick_qs.prompt: A vendor reports work complete, but inspections show gaps. What comes first?

options.A: Accept completion to protect the relationship
options.B: Escalate the vendor to senior leadership
options.C: Wait until contract closure to evaluate the vendor
options.D: Review inspection evidence against contract terms

quick_qs.why: Evidence-based evaluation comes before escalation, and waiting until completion lets unresolved issues grow.

cards.back: Actively manage suppliers during delivery by tracking performance and obligations and handling issues and changes through contract terms, rather than waiting for disputes or closure.
cards.explain: Actively manage suppliers during delivery by tracking performance and obligations and handling issues and changes through contract terms, rather than waiting for disputes or closure.
cards.note: Manage obligations, performance, and changes through contract terms
traps: Letting suppliers manage issues until formal disputes
Handing all supplier communication to procurement alone
Reviewing supplier obligations only at contract closure

quick_qs.prompt: A supplier requests extra payment for retesting caused by its own missed steps. First response?

options.A: Pay it to protect the validation schedule
options.B: Escalate the request to senior leadership
options.C: Review contract terms and change provisions
options.D: Have quality assurance negotiate with the supplier

quick_qs.why: Contract terms, obligations, and change provisions determine the response; paying, escalating, or delegating first skips contract management.

quick_qs.prompt: What is procurement's proper role in managing supplier performance?

options.A: Partner with the PM, using project delivery input
options.B: Handle all supplier communications independently of the PM
options.C: Take over only once a formal dispute arises
options.D: Review obligations only at contract closure

quick_qs.why: Procurement needs project input on delivery and performance; waiting for disputes or closure misses noncompliance during delivery.

cards.front: Quantify risk and contingency financial allocations
cards.back: Size contingency reserves from the analyzed financial exposure of identified risks, not from prior percentages, sponsor preference, or removal to make budgets look attractive.
cards.explain: Size contingency reserves from the analyzed financial exposure of identified risks, not from prior percentages, sponsor preference, or removal to make budgets look attractive.
cards.note: Size contingency from analyzed risk exposure before baselining budget
traps: Using a fixed contingency percentage from a prior project
Letting the sponsor pick contingency from risk tolerance
Removing contingency to make the baseline look attractive

quick_qs.prompt: How should contingency reserves be determined?

options.A: A standard percentage from past projects
options.B: Whatever the sponsor's risk tolerance suggests
options.C: Set by finance after delivery begins
options.D: From analyzed exposure of identified risks

quick_qs.why: Contingency should reflect this project's analyzed risk exposure; prior percentages and sponsor tolerance do not quantify it.

quick_qs.prompt: Why is removing contingency to make the baseline attractive wrong?

options.A: It violates the organization's cost aggregation rules
options.B: It hides risk and weakens financial control
options.C: It requires an earned value recalculation
options.D: It automatically converts reserves into management reserve

quick_qs.why: Removing contingency does not remove risk; it hides exposure and weakens financial control.

cards.front: Monitor financial variations and work with the governance process
cards.back: Validate cost variances against baseline and thresholds, analyze drivers, then route recommendations or budget changes through the agreed governance process and record decisions.
cards.explain: Validate cost variances against baseline and thresholds, analyze drivers, then route recommendations or budget changes through the agreed governance process and record decisions.
cards.note: Validate variance, analyze drivers, recommend options through governance
traps: Requesting funds before validating the variance
Absorbing overruns in contingency without governance review
Reclassifying or moving costs to hide the variance

quick_qs.prompt: A cost variance appears in reporting. What should the project manager do FIRST?

options.A: Validate it against baseline and thresholds
options.B: Request additional funding from the sponsor now
options.C: Cut spending equally across work packages
options.D: Move the overrun into contingency reserve

quick_qs.why: Variance response starts with validation and threshold comparison; funding requests, cuts, or reserve moves before analysis bypass governance.

quick_qs.prompt: After governance approves a cost action, what must the project manager do?

options.A: Tell finance and update artifacts at closure
options.B: Announce the action before documenting it
options.C: Record it and update financial artifacts
options.D: Keep it in meeting notes for reference

quick_qs.why: Governance outcomes must be recorded, reflected in financial artifacts and forecasts, and then communicated.

cards.topic: Plan and optimize quality of products/deliverables
cards.back: Execute the approved quality plan as written: perform planned reviews and inspections, use agreed checklists and metrics, record defects, and verify corrective actions.
cards.explain: Execute the approved quality plan as written: perform planned reviews and inspections, use agreed checklists and metrics, record defects, and verify corrective actions.
cards.note: Apply the quality plan's reviews, metrics, and defect workflow
traps: Deferring quality concerns to final acceptance testing
Replacing planned reviews with informal team checks
Letting developers set defect thresholds independently

quick_qs.prompt: Reviewers use different checklists and defect severity ratings. What should happen?

options.A: Let each team keep its preferred checklist
options.B: Enforce the approved checklists and workflow
options.C: Add more inspections without changing process
options.D: Defer alignment until the final audit

quick_qs.why: Executing the quality plan means consistent use of approved checklists and defect workflows, creating measurable control before more work.

quick_qs.prompt: When should quality concerns found during execution be addressed?

options.A: During final acceptance testing
options.B: At phase closure, once the schedule has recovered
options.C: After release, in a final audit
options.D: Now, through the planned corrective workflow

quick_qs.why: Deferring quality to acceptance, closure, or post-release audits weakens control; the plan's corrective workflow applies during execution.

cards.topic: Plan and optimize quality of products/deliverables
cards.back: When defects recur, analyze root causes and change the process that produces them, then verify the improvement, rather than adding inspection or repeating fixes.
cards.explain: When defects recur, analyze root causes and change the process that produces them, then verify the improvement, rather than adding inspection or repeating fixes.
cards.note: Find root cause, update the process, verify adoption
traps: Adding inspectors without changing upstream process
Fixing each defect again without process change
Logging lessons only, without changing practices

quick_qs.prompt: The same defect recurs despite added end-of-line inspection. What is the best response?

options.A: Add more inspectors at final verification
options.B: Approve extra scrap or rework allowance
options.C: Fix the process that creates the defect
options.D: Record it as a lesson for future projects

quick_qs.why: Continuous improvement prevents recurrence by changing the producing process; more inspection or rework budget only treats symptoms.

quick_qs.prompt: Why is asking people to be more careful a weak improvement action?

options.A: It changes no process that causes defects
options.B: It requires governance approval to enforce
options.C: It increases the cost of conformance
options.D: It conflicts with the retrospective format

quick_qs.why: Improvement means a concrete, measurable process change; exhortation leaves the defect-producing workflow unchanged.

cards.back: Build schedule estimates from comparable historical data and benchmarks, adjusted for context differences, rather than vendor claims, optimism, or waiting for a missed milestone.
cards.explain: Build schedule estimates from comparable historical data and benchmarks, adjusted for context differences, rather than vendor claims, optimism, or waiting for a missed milestone.
cards.note: Estimate from comparable history, adjusted for current conditions
traps: Using vendor brochures or supplier timelines as-is
Pushing staff to commit without reviewing history
Deferring benchmark use until a milestone is missed

quick_qs.prompt: Benchmark data comes from sites with different layouts. What should the project manager do?

options.A: Accept it because the installations look broadly similar
options.B: Discard it and ask staff for dates
options.C: Escalate the uncertainty to procurement
options.D: Assess applicability and adjust for differences

quick_qs.why: Benchmarks help only when their applicability is checked; differences in context must be reflected before using them in the schedule.

quick_qs.prompt: Historical data shows winter night shifts are less productive. How should estimates reflect this?

options.A: Use summer rates, since equipment is the same
options.B: Adjust durations using the seasonal data
options.C: Ask crews to maintain normal productivity
options.D: Revise only if authorities reject the plan

quick_qs.why: Historical productivity under similar conditions makes estimates realistic; ignoring it or waiting for rejection leaves schedule risk unresolved.

cards.back: When the schedule varies from baseline, analyze causes and critical path impact before acting, then recommend recovery options through the governance process.
cards.explain: When the schedule varies from baseline, analyze causes and critical path impact before acting, then recommend recovery options through the governance process.
cards.note: Analyze variance causes and impact; recommend recovery through governance
traps: Escalating the delay before validating variance drivers
Removing quality checks to recover lost time
Moving dates without comparing against control thresholds

quick_qs.prompt: A milestone is three weeks late. What should precede choosing a recovery option?

options.A: Analysis of causes and critical path impact
options.B: Escalation to the sponsor for direction
options.C: Adding overtime or weekend work to recover the delay
options.D: Rebaselining future milestone dates

quick_qs.why: Recovery options depend on understanding variance drivers and critical path impact; escalating or adding work first skips analysis.

quick_qs.prompt: A small variance threatens a fixed regulatory inspection window. What does this show?

options.A: Small variances can be safely ignored
options.B: Only critical path tasks need tracking
options.C: Impact matters more than numeric size
options.D: Variance should be reported only at phase gates

quick_qs.why: Variance analysis assesses consequences, not just magnitude; a small delay can carry outsized risk.

cards.back: Ensure authorized stakeholders can find and use current artifacts through one controlled repository with clear versions, ownership, and role-based access protecting sensitive records.
cards.explain: Ensure authorized stakeholders can find and use current artifacts through one controlled repository with clear versions, ownership, and role-based access protecting sensitive records.
cards.note: Provide controlled, role-based access to current artifacts in one repository
traps: Escalating access confusion before analyzing information needs
Sharing all drafts broadly before checking sensitivity
Waiting for complaints at the next governance meeting

quick_qs.prompt: Stakeholders use outdated local copies of project artifacts. What fixes this?

options.A: Email the updated files to every stakeholder weekly
options.B: Let each workstream keep its own folder
options.C: Share every draft broadly for visibility
options.D: A single controlled source with access rules

quick_qs.why: A single source of truth with access rules and navigation lets stakeholders find current, approved information.

quick_qs.prompt: Confidential contract artifacts are visible to broad audiences. Best response?

options.A: Remove all the contract artifacts from the repository entirely
options.B: Apply role-based access to current versions
options.C: Email sensitive records only to legal
options.D: Escalate to the sponsor before acting

quick_qs.why: Accessibility balances access and protection: confirm confidentiality needs and give role-based access to the latest artifacts.

cards.front: Continually assess the effectiveness of artifact management
cards.back: Regularly assess whether artifacts are current, consistent, and traceable; reconcile contradictions and update dependent artifacts so teams do not act on outdated information.
cards.explain: Regularly assess whether artifacts are current, consistent, and traceable; reconcile contradictions and update dependent artifacts so teams do not act on outdated information.
cards.note: Assess artifact currency; reconcile and update dependent artifacts
traps: Letting users pick whichever artifact suits them
Keeping approved artifacts unchanged despite new information
Escalating before analyzing the artifact gaps

quick_qs.prompt: A risk register was not updated after new inspection findings. What should the PM do?

options.A: Assess currency and update the register
options.B: Let engineers recall findings in meetings
options.C: Replace the register with vendor reports
options.D: Escalate to leadership before any update

quick_qs.why: Artifact effectiveness requires current content; memory or substitute documents create misleading status information.

quick_qs.prompt: Runbooks reference retired network diagrams. What is the core artifact management issue?

options.A: Too many artifacts are being produced by the team
options.B: Operations lacks access to diagrams
options.C: Dependent artifacts were not updated together
options.D: The architecture diagrams are inaccurate

quick_qs.why: When one artifact changes, dependent artifacts must be reviewed and updated so teams act on consistent information.

cards.front: Conclude activities to close the project or phase (e.g., final lessons learned, retrospectives, procurement, financials, resources)
cards.back: Before closing, finish procurement closeout, financial reconciliation, change dispositions, lessons learned, knowledge transfer, and resource release, even if deliverables already operate.
cards.explain: Before closing, finish procurement closeout, financial reconciliation, change dispositions, lessons learned, knowledge transfer, and resource release, even if deliverables already operate.
cards.note: Finish all closure activities before formally closing
traps: Closing because the deliverable is already operational
Releasing the team before lessons learned are done
Deferring invoices or records to operations later

quick_qs.prompt: The system is live but vendor invoices remain open. Can the project close?

options.A: Yes, because the system is operational
options.B: No, financial closure must finish first
options.C: Yes, accounting can settle invoices later
options.D: Yes, if the sponsor approves closure now

quick_qs.why: Operational deliverables are partial completion; procurement and financial closure must be complete before closing.

quick_qs.prompt: When should team members be released at closure?

options.A: As soon as the major deliverables are formally accepted
options.B: Once the sponsor needs them elsewhere
options.C: Before lessons learned, to save cost
options.D: After lessons learned and handover are done

quick_qs.why: Releasing people first loses their knowledge; finish lessons learned and handover, then release resources.

cards.front: Break down situations to identify the root cause of a misunderstanding of the vision
cards.back: When stakeholders interpret the vision differently, facilitate analysis of the assumptions and meanings behind each interpretation before imposing, splitting, or rewording the vision.
cards.explain: When stakeholders interpret the vision differently, facilitate analysis of the assumptions and meanings behind each interpretation before imposing, splitting, or rewording the vision.
cards.note: Facilitate analysis of assumptions behind differing vision interpretations
traps: Asking the sponsor to impose one interpretation
Splitting work so each group follows its view
Rewording the vision before diagnosing the gap

quick_qs.prompt: Two groups describe the project vision differently. What should the PM do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the sponsor to pick one interpretation
options.B: Create separate tracks for each interpretation
options.C: Analyze the assumptions behind each view
options.D: Rewrite the vision to include both views

quick_qs.why: Identify the root cause of the misunderstanding before corrective action; imposing or rewording treats symptoms.

quick_qs.prompt: Why is splitting workstreams by interpretation a poor fix for vision conflict?

options.A: It avoids the conflict without resolving it
options.B: It doubles the overall cost of the project budget
options.C: It requires a new project charter approval
options.D: It violates the team's working agreements

quick_qs.why: Separate tracks fragment understanding instead of building alignment around one shared vision.

cards.front: Communicate conflict management principles with the team and external stakeholders
cards.back: Proactively communicate conflict principles, such as respectful, issue-focused, evidence-based discussion and clear escalation paths, to team and external stakeholders before escalating or separating parties.
cards.explain: Proactively communicate conflict principles, such as respectful, issue-focused, evidence-based discussion and clear escalation paths, to team and external stakeholders before escalating or separating parties.
cards.note: Communicate shared conflict norms and escalation paths to all parties
traps: Escalating behavior to the sponsor first
Excluding or separating the disagreeing parties
Telling one side to manage its own behavior

quick_qs.prompt: Disagreements between internal staff and a vendor are turning personal. First step?

options.A: Ask the vendor lead to manage its staff
options.B: Escalate conduct concerns to the sponsor
options.C: Exclude the vendor from meetings until tension settles
options.D: Restate shared conflict norms to all parties

quick_qs.why: Communicating conflict principles to everyone restores constructive engagement without premature escalation or exclusion.

quick_qs.prompt: Who should receive the project's conflict management principles?

options.A: Only internal team members
options.B: Team and external stakeholders
options.C: Only the parties currently in conflict
options.D: Only managers and the sponsor

quick_qs.why: Conflicts span organizations, so principles must be shared with the team and external stakeholders alike.

cards.back: Empower capable teams by defining decision boundaries, tolerances, and escalation thresholds, then letting them decide within those limits and reviewing outcomes together.
cards.explain: Empower capable teams by defining decision boundaries, tolerances, and escalation thresholds, then letting them decide within those limits and reviewing outcomes together.
cards.note: Set decision boundaries, then let the team decide
traps: Approving every small decision personally
Routing minor decisions to sponsors or steering committees
Granting freedom without any defined boundaries

quick_qs.prompt: Experts keep waiting for PM approval on minor decisions within tolerance. Best response?

options.A: Authorize them to decide within tolerances
options.B: Keep approving until they prove faster
options.C: Send decisions to the steering committee
options.D: Assign one senior lead to make every decision

quick_qs.why: Authority within agreed tolerances empowers those closest to the work; personal or committee approval sustains dependency.

quick_qs.prompt: What keeps team empowerment from becoming a loss of control?

options.A: Project manager approval of every team decision
options.B: Removing all governance from the team
options.C: Clear boundaries with shared outcome review
options.D: Weekly steering committee sign-offs

quick_qs.why: Boundaries plus joint inspection of outcomes preserve alignment while the team owns decisions.

cards.back: Match leadership style to each member's readiness and the situation: coach or direct the inexperienced, delegate to experts, and direct briefly during urgent crises.
cards.explain: Match leadership style to each member's readiness and the situation: coach or direct the inexperienced, delegate to experts, and direct briefly during urgent crises.
cards.note: Assess readiness and adapt leadership style to each need
traps: Using one directive style for everyone
Delegating everything because teams should self-manage
Asking the sponsor to define the leadership style

quick_qs.prompt: A capable team faces an urgent outage requiring fast decisions. Which style fits?

options.A: Laissez-faire, letting the team fully self-organize
options.B: Temporarily directive, to coordinate response
options.C: Democratic, with a full consensus vote
options.D: Coaching, with time for reflection

quick_qs.why: Temporary directive coordination suits urgent response even for capable teams; the style changes back afterward.

quick_qs.prompt: A team mixes experienced developers and new analysts. Best leadership approach?

options.A: Use one directive style for the sake of consistency
options.B: Delegate everything to the developers
options.C: Let developers lead the new analysts
options.D: Delegate to experts, coach the analysts

quick_qs.why: Situational leadership adapts support to capability: delegation for experts, coaching for those still learning.

cards.front: Analyze and tailor communication to stakeholder needs
cards.back: Analyze each stakeholder group's information needs, then tailor content, format, channel, and timing so every audience receives relevant, usable information.
cards.explain: Analyze each stakeholder group's information needs, then tailor content, format, channel, and timing so every audience receives relevant, usable information.
cards.note: Analyze audience needs; tailor content, format, channel, and timing
traps: Sending the same report to every stakeholder
Making stakeholders search repositories for information
Asking one group to relay messages to another

quick_qs.prompt: Executives want risk trends; supervisors need cutover details. What should the PM do?

options.A: Send one detailed report to both groups
options.B: Ask supervisors to read executive summaries
options.C: Tailor separate messages to each group
options.D: Reduce updates until someone asks

quick_qs.why: Different needs require tailored content and format; one report is too technical for some and too vague for others.

quick_qs.prompt: Which is the project manager's responsibility in stakeholder communication?

options.A: Fit messages to each audience's needs
options.B: Let stakeholders find information themselves
options.C: Use one format to keep messaging consistent
options.D: Communicate only when stakeholders request it

quick_qs.why: Pushing responsibility to stakeholders or communicating reactively increases misunderstanding; the PM tailors communication.

cards.back: Categorize stakeholders by influence, interest, impact, and engagement needs so engagement effort is prioritized, rather than treating everyone the same or following politics.
cards.explain: Categorize stakeholders by influence, interest, impact, and engagement needs so engagement effort is prioritized, rather than treating everyone the same or following politics.
cards.note: Categorize stakeholders by influence, interest, impact, and needs
traps: Treating all stakeholders the same
Letting one group define or represent others
Delaying categorization until problems emerge

quick_qs.prompt: Which basis best supports stakeholder categorization for engagement planning?

options.A: Department and reporting line only
options.B: The sponsor's view of political importance
options.C: Who has complained most recently
options.D: Influence, interest, impact, and needs

quick_qs.why: Department-only or political grouping ignores real differences in influence and needs that drive engagement planning.

quick_qs.prompt: A highly impacted group has little decision authority. How should it be treated?

options.A: Deprioritized, since it cannot decide
options.B: Categorized for engagement by its impact
options.C: Represented by a more senior stakeholder group
options.D: Engaged only after rollout begins

quick_qs.why: Impact is a categorization dimension alongside influence; affected groups need their own engagement approach.

cards.front: Identify internal and external customer expectations
cards.back: Identify internal and external customer expectations directly from each group before design decisions, rather than relying on contracts, proxies, or post-launch complaints.
cards.explain: Identify internal and external customer expectations directly from each group before design decisions, rather than relying on contracts, proxies, or post-launch complaints.
cards.note: Elicit expectations directly from internal and external customers early
traps: Relying only on contract language
Letting internal staff speak for external customers
Gathering expectations after launch or first review

quick_qs.prompt: Why shouldn't internal managers represent external customer expectations?

options.A: It filters needs through internal assumptions
options.B: It breaks the project's communications management plan
options.C: It requires approval from procurement
options.D: It makes the stakeholder register too long

quick_qs.why: Proxies filter external needs through internal assumptions; direct engagement reveals expectations documents miss.

quick_qs.prompt: When should internal and external customer expectations be identified?

options.A: After the first deliverable review meeting is held
options.B: During pilot use, from complaints
options.C: Before design and requirements decisions
options.D: Once the prototype is available

quick_qs.why: Late discovery creates avoidable rework; identify expectations before design or requirements are finalized.

cards.back: Capture critical, especially tacit, knowledge from contributors using structured methods before they leave or work proceeds, because documents and informal sharing miss key details.
cards.explain: Capture critical, especially tacit, knowledge from contributors using structured methods before they leave or work proceeds, because documents and informal sharing miss key details.
cards.note: Capture contributor knowledge through structured sessions before departure
traps: Relying on informal sharing when time allows
Treating final documents as the only source
Waiting until experts leave or workflows are built

quick_qs.prompt: Experts will soon leave the project. What is the best knowledge-gathering approach?

options.A: Ask them to share informally when time allows
options.B: Run structured capture sessions now
options.C: Rely on the final project documents
options.D: Contact them later if questions arise

quick_qs.why: Structured gathering before departure preserves useful knowledge; informal or later attempts risk losing it.

quick_qs.prompt: Why aren't final project documents enough for knowledge transfer?

options.A: They are usually too long to read
options.B: They need formal PMO approval before any release
options.C: They are archived after project closure
options.D: They miss tacit, judgment-based knowledge

quick_qs.why: Documents capture explicit facts but not the practical judgment and workarounds experts carry.

cards.back: Set up a structured, recurring feedback loop that captures input from affected stakeholders, reviews patterns, acts on them, and tells contributors what changed.
cards.explain: Set up a structured, recurring feedback loop that captures input from affected stakeholders, reviews patterns, acts on them, and tells contributors what changed.
cards.note: Create structured feedback capture, review, action, and response
traps: Collecting feedback only after final delivery
Relying on ad hoc or sponsor-only feedback
Not telling contributors which changes were made

quick_qs.prompt: Participation in feedback drops because contributors see no response. What is missing?

options.A: A larger feedback survey sample
options.B: More frequent stakeholder status meetings
options.C: Closing the loop with contributors
options.D: Sponsor review of all feedback

quick_qs.why: A feedback loop includes acting on input and responding; without visible response, contributors disengage.

quick_qs.prompt: Feedback arrives by email, hallway talk, and meetings. What should the PM do first?

options.A: Set up one structured intake and review
options.B: Respond to each comment as it arrives
options.C: Wait to collect feedback at final delivery
options.D: Use only the sponsor's comments formally

quick_qs.why: Structured intake reveals recurring, high-impact patterns that scattered or ad hoc feedback hides.

cards.front: Describe and establish the structure, rules, procedures, reporting, ethics, and policies through the use of organizational process assets (OPAs)
cards.back: Use organizational process assets to establish consistent governance structure, decision rights, procedures, reporting, ethics rules, and policies instead of local or informal practices.
cards.explain: Use organizational process assets to establish consistent governance structure, decision rights, procedures, reporting, ethics rules, and policies instead of local or informal practices.
cards.note: Establish governance rules and procedures from existing OPAs
traps: Letting each workstream set its own rules
Escalating every decision without defined thresholds
Creating new rules without checking existing policies

quick_qs.prompt: Workstreams use different approval thresholds for the same change type. Best fix?

options.A: Let each team keep local thresholds
options.B: Escalate all approvals to the sponsor
options.C: Have the PMO review after delivery
options.D: Set common rules using the OPAs

quick_qs.why: Consistent governance comes from shared rules built on OPAs; local rules, blanket escalation, or late review leave gaps.

quick_qs.prompt: What should a project manager check before creating new governance rules?

options.A: The team's preferred working style
options.B: Existing organizational policies and OPAs
options.C: The vendor's own internal governance procedures
options.D: Recent decisions made by executives

quick_qs.why: OPAs supply approved procedures, templates, and policies; new rules created without them cause inconsistency.

cards.back: Classify compliance obligations into distinct categories, such as regulatory, safety, privacy, and contractual, so owners, reviewers, and priorities can be assigned and reported.
cards.explain: Classify compliance obligations into distinct categories, such as regulatory, safety, privacy, and contractual, so owners, reviewers, and priorities can be assigned and reported.
cards.note: Classify obligations into compliance categories with accountable owners
traps: Keeping all obligations in one undifferentiated list
Assigning every obligation to a single function
Deferring classification until auditors ask

quick_qs.prompt: Why classify compliance requirements into categories?

options.A: To assign owners and reviewers clearly
options.B: To reduce the total number of obligations
options.C: To let auditors define project priorities
options.D: To move obligations to individual vendors

quick_qs.why: Categories show which specialists, authorities, and owners must validate each obligation and support risk-based prioritization.

quick_qs.prompt: When should compliance obligations be categorized?

options.A: When auditors first request evidence
options.B: After a jurisdiction rejects a submission
options.C: Early, before assigning owners and work
options.D: During final compliance testing

quick_qs.why: Delaying classification leaves ownership ambiguous; categorize early so compliance work can be planned and monitored.

cards.front: Determine the necessary approach and action(s) to address compliance needs
cards.back: When a compliance gap appears, determine corrective actions, evidence, owners, and schedule impacts before release, rather than proceeding, deferring, or escalating first.
cards.explain: When a compliance gap appears, determine corrective actions, evidence, owners, and schedule impacts before release, rather than proceeding, deferring, or escalating first.
cards.note: Define corrective compliance actions and impacts before proceeding
traps: Proceeding because most items already pass
Waiting for regulators or complaints to find gaps
Using manual workarounds instead of fixing the gap

quick_qs.prompt: Missing compliance evidence is found just before go-live. What should the PM do?

options.A: Go live and collect evidence afterward
options.B: Define recovery, retest, and acceptance actions
options.C: Accept the contractor's verbal confirmation instead
options.D: Escalate to executives before defining options

quick_qs.why: The PM analyzes the gap and determines corrective and evidence actions; shortcuts or premature escalation leave exposure.

quick_qs.prompt: Why is waiting for complaints a poor response to a known compliance gap?

options.A: Complaints are hard to categorize and track
options.B: It overloads the support desk
options.C: It delays the release schedule
options.D: Exposure grows while the gap persists

quick_qs.why: Deferring compliance action increases exposure to avoidable risk; determine and apply corrective actions now.

cards.front: Implement approved changes to the project
cards.back: Once a change is approved, update all affected plans, backlogs, tests, procurement, and communications, then execute it with clear ownership, without delay or re-escalation.
cards.explain: Once a change is approved, update all affected plans, backlogs, tests, procurement, and communications, then execute it with clear ownership, without delay or re-escalation.
cards.note: Update affected plans and execute the approved change
traps: Continuing the original plan after approval
Re-escalating an already approved change
Implementing without updating tests or documentation

quick_qs.prompt: A change was approved by the change control board. What should the PM do next?

options.A: Escalate again to confirm the decision
options.B: Wait for the next release cycle
options.C: Update affected plans and execute it
options.D: Let the vendor define the change scope

quick_qs.why: Approved changes must be reflected in plans and executed with control; re-escalation or delay leaves work misaligned.

quick_qs.prompt: In agile delivery, implementing an approved change mainly means updating what?

options.A: The backlog and sprint plan
options.B: The project charter and business case
options.C: The organizational process assets
options.D: The stakeholder register only

quick_qs.why: Approved agile changes flow through the backlog, acceptance criteria, and sprint planning.

cards.front: Determine and apply an intervention strategy to remove/minimize impediments
cards.back: Remove impediments actively by analyzing them and applying a collaborative intervention, such as facilitating decisions, finding alternatives, or resequencing, before escalating or waiting.
cards.explain: Remove impediments actively by analyzing them and applying a collaborative intervention, such as facilitating decisions, finding alternatives, or resequencing, before escalating or waiting.
cards.note: Facilitate a collaborative intervention to remove the blocker
traps: Escalating to executives before exploring options
Waiting until the blocker resolves itself
Bypassing controls or pushing work onto others

quick_qs.prompt: Two vendors dispute ownership of a blocking defect. Best intervention?

options.A: Assign it to whichever vendor the users see
options.B: Escalate the dispute to executives immediately
options.C: Suspend testing until they agree
options.D: Facilitate joint triage and assign ownership

quick_qs.why: The PM facilitates joint triage to clear the blocker; assigning by visibility, escalating, or waiting stalls testing.

quick_qs.prompt: A required reviewer is unavailable for two weeks. What protects both progress and compliance?

options.A: Developers self-certify until they return
options.B: Arrange alternate qualified reviewers
options.C: Mark the items done and revisit later
options.D: Escalate before checking any alternatives

quick_qs.why: Find alternate qualified resources and adjust timing; bypassing compliance checks or escalating first is not intervention.

cards.back: Identify risks early and broadly across technical, people, supplier, regulatory, and schedule areas with stakeholders, before baselining, purchasing, or sequencing work.
cards.explain: Identify risks early and broadly across technical, people, supplier, regulatory, and schedule areas with stakeholders, before baselining, purchasing, or sequencing work.
cards.note: Run broad risk identification with stakeholders before committing
traps: Planning first and adding risks later
Focusing on only one visible risk type
Letting a vendor or team own all risk identification

quick_qs.prompt: When should risk identification happen relative to approving the baseline?

options.A: Before approving the baseline
options.B: After execution reveals real risks
options.C: Only when the sponsor requests it
options.D: During retrospectives after release

quick_qs.why: Risk identification precedes baseline, procurement, and sequencing decisions so exposure is managed proactively.

quick_qs.prompt: Why is documenting only fraud risks on a payments release a weak practice?

options.A: Fraud risks belong to compliance
options.B: Fraud risks are usually low impact
options.C: It leaves other risk areas unseen
options.D: It must wait for backlog priority

quick_qs.why: Focusing on the most visible risk bypasses disciplined evaluation of other uncertain events affecting objectives.

cards.front: Maintain a risk register (e.g., poor IT security)
cards.back: Treat the risk register as a living document: update probability, impact, owners, triggers, and responses as soon as new information changes exposure.
cards.explain: Treat the risk register as a living document: update probability, impact, owners, triggers, and responses as soon as new information changes exposure.
cards.note: Update register exposure, owners, triggers, and responses now
traps: Keeping original entries because the risk was identified
Tracking risks informally or outside the register
Waiting for a workshop or event before updating

quick_qs.prompt: Failed patch testing changes an existing IT security risk. What should happen?

options.A: Keep the original entry unchanged
options.B: Update the register entry now
options.C: Let IT support track it separately
options.D: Escalate before touching the register

quick_qs.why: New evidence changes exposure, so the register must be updated immediately; stale or off-register tracking misleads decisions.

quick_qs.prompt: Which risk register elements should be revised when exposure changes?

options.A: Only the risk title and its category label
options.B: Only the probability score, nothing else
options.C: Only the risk owner's contact details
options.D: Exposure, owner, triggers, and responses

quick_qs.why: Changed conditions can alter probability, impact, ownership, triggers, and responses; update all affected fields.

cards.front: Help ensure continuous improvement processes are updated
cards.back: Turn lessons into updated organizational processes, checklists, templates, and playbooks so future work avoids repeating problems, rather than archiving notes or waiting for recurrence.
cards.explain: Turn lessons into updated organizational processes, checklists, templates, and playbooks so future work avoids repeating problems, rather than archiving notes or waiting for recurrence.
cards.note: Update the relevant process asset with the lesson
traps: Archiving the lesson without changing processes
Relying on people to remember next time
Waiting for the problem to recur

quick_qs.prompt: A review finds the procurement checklist lacks supplier confirmation triggers. Next step?

options.A: Keep it; the next supplier may do better
options.B: Ask staff to track deliveries separately
options.C: Update the checklist with the triggers
options.D: Wait to see if the issue repeats

quick_qs.why: Continuous improvement means updating the reusable process asset now; waiting or workarounds let the gap repeat.

quick_qs.prompt: Why is storing retrospective notes without changing practices insufficient?

options.A: Future work will repeat the same problem
options.B: Notes must be approved by the PMO first
options.C: Retrospectives are not official artifacts
options.D: It breaks the change control process

quick_qs.why: Lessons only help when they change standard processes that future teams actually use.

cards.front: Survey changes to the external business environment (e.g., regulations, technology, geopolitical, market)
cards.back: Proactively scan external changes in regulations, technology, markets, and geopolitics, and assess their relevance to the project before finalizing related decisions.
cards.explain: Proactively scan external changes in regulations, technology, markets, and geopolitics, and assess their relevance to the project before finalizing related decisions.
cards.note: Survey external changes and assess project impact before deciding
traps: Ignoring draft or announced changes until enforced
Handing external changes to other functions outside planning
Waiting for shortages or churn to confirm impact

quick_qs.prompt: Regulators publish draft guidance affecting planned submissions. What should the PM do?

options.A: Finalize, since drafts are not enforceable
options.B: Let regulatory affairs handle it separately
options.C: Escalate it before reviewing relevance
options.D: Assess its relevance before finalizing

quick_qs.why: Draft or announced changes can still affect the project; survey and assess relevance before committing decisions.

quick_qs.prompt: When should external environment changes be surveyed?

options.A: After component shortages affect delivery dates
options.B: Before finalizing related project decisions
options.C: Once the new rule becomes effective
options.D: Only during annual budget cycles

quick_qs.why: Waiting for effects or effective dates leaves exposure unmanaged; scan before procurement, design, or backlog decisions.
